div.p: RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. THER'S NOWT AS QUARE AS FOOAK. We read o'er quare things oft i' books; An' wondrous finds i' ineawldy nooks, 0' fossils, coins, an' shells. These stray bits ov owd times gone by Are treasured up an' kept on t' sly ; Bud wod abeawt eawrsels ? We're t' quarest things, as t' world con show; I' o th' museums give a co, I' nook au' ruins pooak, An' after o yo'r huntin's done, Yo'll find ther's nowt below th' breet sun At's hawf as guars as fooak !

If summat turns up to yo'r gaze A relic rude ov other days, At's eawt o' date an' strange, Yo'll sooart, iv thowtfully inclined, It use an' porpus, yo'r mind, An' wonder at th' gret change I' th' big world, sin 'twur chucked aside; An wod a mighty ratched-eawt stride, I' th' land o' British oak, Progression's med sin id wur new. That's quare, but then—gi'e truth id due,— Ther's nowt as quare as fooak! A wander, hewed fro' t' solid rock, May touch eawr nerves wi' sudden shock, An' mek us think o'er V past; But sitch like dull, cowd, lifeless things, Tho' they cause strange imaginin's, Ther meanin's soon o'ercast. Tho' th' earth gi'es mony a gem to t' seet, As on id hist'ry flings a lest, Yet monkind's faces clooak Them deep desires as lurk i' th' heart. An' mek 'em act a double part— Hey! nowt's as quare as fooak! Ther's sum as seem like earthly saints. Hypocrisy each " phizog ' paints, An' weel they keep up t' sham. Lots booast they're leadin' Christian lives, An' tho' ther conscience cuts like knives, Con let ther parents clam! An' sum, brimful o' mek-believe, They'll grin an' titter i' ther sleeve, An' reckon id a jooak To praise chaps to ther face, an' then Backbite 'em to ther fella men— Ay! nowt's as quare as fooak! Sum cry eawt poverty, an' bleed Ih'ed kornd be spared fro' them i' need, To mek ther bank books swell; But wed deceit an' fraud ther is, Wod dodges and rascalities, / Ther's nooan but ONE con tell. Fooak hid ther thowts wV heop'd-up wards, An' Self s o theer when chance affoards, To do a maister strooak. Th' world's upside deawn, forth' wayk prove strong, Truth's med t' liar, Reight's co'd wrong, But—no set's as quare as fooak! JACK 0' ANN'S.

A Flour Garden—A -wheat field. A Fine Building—A police court. Advice to Purchasers of Forster's Life—Reid it. A local poet begins an apostrophe to the ocean with "Prodigious dampness." A sign on a small house in the vicinity of Dublin, a few years ago, had this inscription:—" Asses' milk every morning bat from the cow." Wife: "Why is it, John, that you rarely kiss me now? Before we were married you bothered me almost to death." Husband: I know it, my dear, and I laid in stock enough to last." Editor's young Wife: My dear, you must pardon me for coming down in a wrapper this morning." Editor: "Don't mention it, my love. Some of our most valued articles come to us in wrappers." A witty old physician, on meeting a neighbour's ducks in the road, was saluted with the usual "quack, quack, quack." " See here," he cried to the neighbour, "keep these ducks at home, or I'll shoot 'em. They're indulging in personal remarks." A timid youth had business with a firm consisting of two brothers. Finding one f them alone in the counting room, he stammered out: " P-p-p-p-please, sir,h-h-h-have I the h-h-honour of ad-d-d-dressing you, or y-y-y-your b-b-b-brother ?" "My brother, sir," was the uncom- promising reply. A SODDEN AT-TACK—He dropped on his knees at her feet and began the speech he had so long been rehearsing, "Darling love. I hate—l mean, darling, hate, I love you, no—no—l mean " Here his face assumed a livid hue and began to tie itself in hard knots. "What is it— paralysis?" she asked, frantically. " No, love," he 'whispered lioarsely,"l am kneeling on a tack !" - - Arthur who is forbidden to speak at the table, had his revenge the other day, says Harper's Young People. As dinner began he was uneasy, and finally said, "Ma, can't I speak just one word ? " 'You know the rule, Arthur." "Not one word ? " 4` No, Arthur. not until your father finishes the paper." Arthur subsided until the paper was finished, when he was asked what he wished to say. " Oh, nothing ; only Nora put the custards outside the window to cool, and the cat has been eating them up." Very funny mistakes occur when a letter drops out of its place. A few instances folio* :—" In a penny dread- ful—' The beautiful maiden looked into her lover's eyes, and, lashing deeply, said, &c., &c.' In an Irish love ballad—' And rit take thee, dear ass, to my heart.' In a religious book—' We shall all be hanged in the twinkling of an eye.' In a novel—' He arose and shook off his ears.' In a restaurant dinner-carte—' Old fowl.' In a newspaper—` A surgeon was caught last week in the Solent, and sold for 6d. a pound.' In a volume of poems A sense makes the heart grow fonder.' For the italicised words, in this order, read—' Blushing,' 'lass,' changed," fears," cold,' sturgeon,' and' absence.'" A MODEST Dom-R.—A physician who had put his pro- fessional card into a country paper, requested the editor to give him a notice. "Just sit down there at the desk, Doc., and write out what you want," said the editor. Oh, dear, no; I can't write about myself." "I think you can. Just give me the points, if you are too modest to say what you want, and I will throw in the necessary strength." The doctor sat down, and after much splutter- ing, produced the following modest piece of work : " Dr. Abe Collier, whose card we print to-day, is, without doubt, the finest physician in our city. He is a perfect gentleman, and is one of the best surgeons in our city, if not the best His charges are reasonable for a man who , never loses a case, and we are glad to know that he has refused a lucrative practice in another town in order to ' remain in oar city, where he is so highly esteemed for his skill and gentlemanly qualities. He is not an old man, but he is thoroughly experienced, and rarely loses a case. We congratulate the people of our enterprising and beautitul city that he will remain in our city. His office hours are from morning until night when not engaged, and this of itself is an accommodation to the people of our city." A late reverend gentleman who resided in Yorkshire, and was as well known for his eccentricity as his talents, one day Sent his son, a lazy lad about twelve years of age, to catch his horse. The lad went sauntering along, *with a grain of corn in one hand and the bridle in'the other, dragging the reins along the ground. "Thomas," said the father, calling after him in a very solemn tone of voice, "come here, Thomas; I want to say a word to you before you go." The lad returned, and the parson proceeded—" You know, Thomas, that I gave you a great deal of counsel. You know that I have taught you, before closing your eyes, to say, • Now I lay me , down to sleep, !sc.,' beside a good many other things in the way of explanation and advice. But this is the last opportunity I may ever have of speaking to you. I ceuldn't let it pass without giving you my parting charge. Be a good boy, and always say that pretty prayer before going to sleep. 1 fear I shall never see you again." As he said this in a very sad and solemn manner the poor boy began to be frightened, and burst into tears. with this exclamation—" You'll never see me again, pa?" "No; for I shall probably die before you get hack with the horse." This quickened Thomas's ideas, and gathering up the reins, he ran and caught the horse in less time than he had ever done before. SCOTCH BULLS.—Perhaps one of the most curious is the exclamation of the wife after she had heard for the first time the story of the Fall of Man. "Well," said she, "he mun a been a silly eerie, that Adam! Now, if It had been oor Andrew that was placed in the Garden o' Eden he would have been there yet, for, as sure as death, he didna care a dite for apples." A well known anecdote aptly illustrates the same artifice. This is the story of the woman who, having complained to the minister of the offences of her husband, and being re- minded of the duty of forgiveness and of the Apostle's injunction to heap burning coals on his head, answered, "If you think so I'll try it. I've used boiling water often enough, but if you're of opeellion that hot coals would be better—" But in these instances the effect is broad. We get the finest aroma when the point is more narrowly missed. Here is an actual occurrence from unwritten history. After Thomas Carlyle's funeral a very warm admirer of the prophet loosed up the Ecclefechan cottage where he was born. It was not a a show-place then, but the home of a quiet peasant family. The woman, not yet inured to the ways of pil- grims, showed the house as if to an inquiring tenant. Among other things, she pointed out the box bed in whien Thomas was born. "And was Carlyle actually born in that there?" asked the youthful and awe-struck visitor. "Aye, that was he," said the wife, and then complacently added, as though giving still more impor- tant information, "An' oor Maggie was born there, WO." EXECUTING A HEN. BY SYGIL.

Now I am a great believer in and advocate of capital punishment, that is with regard to other people. lam convinced that a bit of hanging does some people good, besides being a boon to the community at large. I think that when a murderer has been dangling at the end of a rope for about an hour, with the prison bell ringing in his ears, he will be a hardened wretch indeed if he does not see the error of his ways and make up his mind that he will "never do it again." I am sure that, were I placed in that exceedingly uncomfortable position, it would throw a gloom over the remainderj of my; life, and cause me to have a wish to discontinue the subject. My imagination occasionally takes curious flights, and sometimes places me in very uncomfortablo positions— imaginary positions. I never could imagine com- mitting murder, but I have, in imagination, placed my- self in a condemned cell, with the imaginary prospect of Berry, the hangman' having to operate upon me the next morning, and I have come to the conclusion that my constitution is so very delicate I could not stand it. My natural modesty would cause me to shrink from the ordoal. I daresay some people would call it cowardice, but whatever they might call it I feel that it would be too much for me. I have, in consequence, decided that I will not commit murder, so that anyone who has hitherto felt intimidated at my fierce aspect may, in future, rest assured that he is safe. Some people advocate the abolition of capital punish- ment. I myself believe that if we were to abolish it, we should destroy the greatest of all deterrents to crime. There is nothing so sacred as life, and there is nothing that a man values above life, therefore, if a person takes the life of a human being, let him pay the highest penalty, even if it is only in the interests of society. Now, my opinion is that if we look at the question with regard to a hereafter, the punishment is not ade- quate to the crime, for the victim is hurried into the presence of his Maker without a moment's warning, whereas the fiend who has robbed him of his dearest possession has time allowed him to arrange his worldly matters, and to secure a " boost "in the realms of bliss, where his sins will be all washed away and he will be as white and as pure as the driven snow. Ugh ! It strikes me as being a pretty and affecting sight to see the culprit, after he has been sentenced to death for committing a dastardly crime upon some inoffensive woman or man, being coddled and pandered to by everybody who goes near him. The warders are in- structed, I suppose, to give him anything in reason to eat or drink. A parson is delegated to show him the way to join the ranks of the pure and undefiled, while his victim may have gone to perdition for anything he cared, and perhaps cares. And isn't it really nice and edifying to read of the conversations he has with his relatives, and to read the letters of advice and repen- tance which he sends to them, and which almost always get into the papers ? But it is a little remarkable that this repentance and sapience never show themselves until after all hope of reprieve is lost and the hang- man's rope is as good as about the repentant's neck. Then what a saint he becomes and what advice he lavishes upon everybody with whom he comes in contact.

There is something within me that rebels against the taking of the life of almost any creature, unless, per- haps, it is in self defence. I don't even like to kill a beetle. Great lands! I've killed millions. Some few years ago I lived at a house where a colony of them had been left by the previous tenant, who had evidently been a collector of the insects such as a curator preserves in glass cases at the Free Library. lam not one to look a gift horse in the mouth, but somehow I did not seem to appreciate the favour. I resented the thought which forced itself upon me that those insects had a kind of prescriptive right to their present abode, because it made me feel as if myself and family were only lodgers, they having lived there long before we did, and having never been evicted. Certainly they were an unobtru- sive tribe, for we saw nothing of them for a few nights; but by-and-bye we began to make their acquaintance. Their native modesty, however, clung to them even to the last, for if we turned a light suddenly upon them they would scamper off with all haste to their hidden retreats. We came to blows. I had the advantage in size, but they beat me hollow in numbers. How I did ravel in their destruction. Yes, I, with my tender nature, did my best to slaughter the lot. Many a time and oft have I rushed in amongst them, and danced the cancan, the highland fling, or an Indian war dance, or a mixture of them all. I can easily imagine that those who escaped were convulsed with laughter at my antics. They knew that victory was with them, bless you! for the more I killed the faster they came. Yes, after slaying millions of them and spending a small fortune in fancy foods for them, I acknowledged myself de- feated, and fled. They cleared me out, hag and baggage. But I am forgetting that this sketch is all about killing a hen. Some little time ago I wrote my experiences as a poultry speculator, giving a history of my hens, at the conclusion of which I said that some day I would give an account of their slaughter. It is only necessary to describe the slaughter of one, for I hired an executioner for the remainder and sold them. Now, as it is quite possible that nobody read my poultry spec. sketch, and as it is also very likely that if anyone did read it they will have forgetten it, I will consider it necessary to state that at the time I am now speaking of I had been a poultry keeper about four months, and had not made a fortune by the speculation. I had fed those fowls upon all kinds of foods, but hal never got to see the colour of their eggs, so, it being Christmas time, and the Missis being in bed poorly, I bethought me suddenly one day that I would kill a hen myself and cook it, and give the Missis a treat. I ought to state here that both myself and the Missis are of an affectionate nature, and we had got to looking upon our hens as members of the family. We had watched those hens--there were four of them - many an hour. We had fed them, and watched them, and made their nests, and arranged them until they had become quite homely and used to us. Such an interest had we taken in them that we had given them each a name. Their names were Aisle, Mary, Alice Ann, and Julia, and we always spoke of them by these names. Such ex- pressions as the following were common :—" Alice Ann doesn't look well to-day; she seems quite sackless about something ;" or "Julia looks in good form this morning. I think she's going to lay an egg ;" or "Mary's cold is worse to-day; she keeps sneezing." I think they all had chronic influenza, for I never saw such hens in all my life for sneezing. They nearly sneezed their bills off sometimes. Such a watery-eyed lot I never saw. Mary turned out to be a man hen, and as saon as she ic that out she began to hector over the others, and to trample and put on them. A hen keeper who came to look at them one day told me that Mary was of the Coach-in-China breed. Ailse was also a foreigner, he said, but I am not quite sure whether he said she was a 1 Mussulman or a Brahmin, but I think he said Brahmin. But of whatever breed she was she was very idle, and 1 she grew nearly too stout to walk, and she sneezed with a voice like a railway train in danger. I believe that Ailse's obesity cost her her life, for it was that that caused me to think she would make some good chicken , troth. Well, as I remarked before, I had the Missis poorly in bed. It was Monday afternoon and a holiday with me. I was looking disconsolately at the hens in the back garden, and ruminating on their happy lot, when the idea suddenly struck me that Ailse would make some splendid chicken broth, that would do the Missis a power of good—and myself as well. For a minute or so it seemed to be a lucky thought, then I asked myself what Ailse had done amiss that she should be sacrificed. Then again I asked myself what she had done to prove her right to be spared. She had never laid a single egg since I bought her; in fact, she had done nothing but eat, drink, end sneeze since I made her acquaintance. Yea, she had grown fat, and that proved to me that she was in a proper condition to be killed. I decided that Ailse must die. She seemed to know it as soon as I had made up my mind, for she got on her feet in a disturbed sort of way, and began to walk slowly about the hen pen, clucking miserably. As soon as I had fully and finally made up my mind that I would kill Ailse, I became unhappy and excited.

I hadn't courage to look her in the face, for I felt sure that she would see guilt in my eye, if I did. I could feel the beating of my heart accelerated, so I took a walk the length of the garden and back to calm myself. I didn't find any calm so I went back again, with the same re- sult. I found that the longer I put the job off the more perturbed I became, and I concluded that if I did not do the deed without delay it would get postponed in- definitely. Then I bethought me that I didn't know how to kill a hen, for I had never killed one before. I thought of a few ways of doing it, but I rejected them one after another. If I had had a gun I would have shot her, but I hadn't, so that was out of the question. Drowning her in a dolly-tub suggested itself, but I thought that would be too much like a natural death, so I rejected that method. I thought next about poison, and that seemed a good idea, but, after a little reflection, I came to the conclusion that if I poisoned her and we ate her afterwards we might join her in the sweet by-and-bye a little sooner than we wanted. I gave up the idea of poison. I would have knocked her on the head if she had had any size of a head to knock at, but there didn't seem to be any knocking -place. My next idea was to chop her head clean off, but it would have taken two people to do that, one to hold her and the other to chop. I was be- ginning to feel a bit used up and tired of the job when I remembered having, as a boy, seen a man on the market take a hen by the" scuft " of the neck and give it (the hen) two or three circular trips in the circurnnambient air, then throw it on the ground, where it made a few spasmodic jerks and "threw up the sponge." "That's it !" I exclaimed aloud," I might have thought of that at first." I got off the garden seat where I had been sitting, and my courage rose. No it didn't, it fell, for I now found myself face to face with the job. I leaned on the rails of the pen and had-a final look at Ailse before tackling her. I thought it was a great pity that she must needs die, but then it is the fate of all hens, so why should I be squeamish about it? While I was looicing at her she gave a shrill sneeze that fairly made me jump. It sounded as if she screamed "Get away ! I got away. I walked the length of the garden again, and I worked myself to such a pitch that I felt fairly desperate walked into that pen at once, and made up the hole in the cote so that she could not escape through it. I needn't have troubled for she was almost too lazy to walk. Then I made a swoop for Ailse, and caught her, and, taking hold of her head, I operated upon her as I had seen the man operate when I was a boy, then threw her on to the ground, and rushed out of the pen and into the house.

After committing the deed I felt anything but com- fortable, and I almost wished I had not engaged in the job at all. I sat me down in the house, for, I should think, fully ten minutes. Then I went to the bick door and opened it gently, and "pept" out to see if anything was moving. All was calm and quiet, so I walked to the hen-pen to survey the battlefield. When I got there Ailse was sitting on her haunches as usual. Great stars I was horrified. Could it be possible that, after what I had put her and myself through, she could still be in the land of the living. I said, "Shoosh !" She didn't shoosh worth a bodle, but she moved sufficiently to convince me that she was tt all alive oh." I was in a mess now, for I felt that I had proceeded so far that retreat was entirely out of the question. Well, without going further into details which would lacerate my own feelings, and perhaps shock those of the more delicate of my readers, I will briefly state that I operated once more upon Ailse without seeming to injure her in the slightest, and from what I have learnt since I feel sure that did not injure her. But my imagination was so excited that the perspiration fairly ran off me. I got so desperate that I decided to hang her, which I did from a clothes-line with a piece of cord.

When I looked at Ailse for the last time, as she was hanging, she had one eye towards me. If I live till I die I shall never forget the expression of that eye, no,never ! I can see it yet ; and I don't think I shall ever lose sight of it. In all my lonely moments that dark mournful eye is present to my view. It expresses no revengeful feelings, no, there is nothing but tender reproach in it ; and it stands in front of my mind's eye like a jewel which has lost its brilliant lustre.

I did manage to pluck Ailse and to cut her up, but I never experienced such loathing, at any time, over any- thing. She was still warm when I cut her up, and that, I fancy, didn't improve my feelings any. And such fat she had about her! The table upon which I cut her up was as if an oilcask had been emptied upon it, and while I was boiling her I skimmed a pint of fat off the broth. I never tasted the broth, though, nor any por- tion of Ailse herself, for I felt anything but hungry, but I seasoned the lot as well as I knew how, and when I saw that it was cooked sufficiently, I tool the Missis a basinful upstairs. The Missis ate ever so mush of the broth, and Ailse, and pronounced them splendid. She then asked me where I had bought the chicken. I said, "I didn't buy it." "Where did you get it then?" she asked. I said, "Out of our own yard. It is one of our own hens.''

I was very indiscreet in telling her, for she went as white as the inside of the basin she was holding, and she said, "Oh, my gracious ! which of them ?" " Ailse," I said, "you know she was no—" I just stepped aside in time, for the broth she had flew about the room.and bed in all directions. She cried about poor Ailse, and she ordered me to bury the remainder of the broth in the garden. I buried it in the ashpit. The hen suffered I know, but if it suffered a quarter of what I did, it was to be pitied indeed. j

HER BROTHER'S KEEPER.
BY MRS. J. K. SPENDER,
Author of "Mr. Nobody," "Parted Lives,' "Both in the 'Wrong," " Recollections of a Country Doctor," "Trust Me," &c.
CHAPTER 11. ST. AGATHA'S MANOR HOUSE.

A clever child much contradicted is apt to become pertinacious. And when the voice of the cuckoo was heard again in the fields, and a rich treat of vocal harmony woke Mrs. Campion from her troubled sleep Ursula talked more than ever of the enchanted palace where the grandmotherwith the silver locks dwelt who had golden stars on her raiment. Everything seemed so suddenly to have yielded to the magic wand of an enchanter, that it was easier to be- lieve in fairy palaces in spring days when the air was no longer crisp and clear but odorous with the breath of cowslips. The child, with her usual shrewdness, had been putting two and two together, and made many curious guesses concerning the fabulous fairy. No doubt she inhabited that large house which she had seen in the distance when she and her little brother had wandered farther than usual one day and had , caught sight of gabled roofs, and pretty old mullioned , windows on which the sunlight sparkled like dia- monds. It could be seen above the trees of a park into which they had not dared to venture. They had inquired the name of the dwelling, and had been told it was St. Agatha's manor house. By force of long conversations on the subject, and much pumping of Peggy, the brother and sister arrived at the conclusion that the dwelling was actually tenanted by a superhuman being, rich as a princess, silver-haired, with a silver wand, and iden- tical no doubt with the fairy grandmother. The curiosity of the boy at last overcame his fear. "Why don't we go and see her," he asked, with wide open eyes, one day. " Stoopid, retorted the girl, astonished at his boldness; "don't you see that if we were to offend the fairy she might change us into stones, or trees, or anything she pleases ! " Ray took fright after this, never mentioning the tabooed subject. And Ursula was a little terrified at the recollection of her own irreverence. Had they not seen smoke issuing from the chimneys of the lodge just within the iron gates, and did not a di agon guard the entrance of these enchanted palaces? This idea was favoured by the fact that Peggy always spoke with a sort of awe of St. Agatha's manor house, and when her charge had asked _ her something about the park had once re- torted in a passion that she would "as lief see them be torn up by wild beasts as go near that place." It was difficult to venture on more direct inquiries, for Peggy refused to answer them. But why should the old woman be silent if she were not herself afraid of the enchantments of the fairy. Why should she caution the children never to wander in the direc- tion of St. Agatha's valley if she, too, were not in deadly fear of the dragon who guarded the entrance to the park? But one morning' when everything that was young and bright seemed to be holiday keeping, Ursula's own nomadic propensities got the better of her. The seam which Peggy had set her to sew while the old woman was tending her mother seemed to be in- terminable, so too did the column of spelling over which Ray was whimpering. "If you will be a good boy," she said suddenly, at the end of her patience after some furtive glances at the door, "we'll go and see the fairy grandmother." Ray's eyes brightened at the idea. "You are not afraid?" she asked, brushing the dirt from his shabby clothes, with the patronising air of a woman of forty, "the fairy could give you a fine new velvet suit with one touch of her wand. We'll take some sweetmeats for the dragon ;" she added triumphantly, giving him a glimpse of some chocolates in her pocket. "Will the dragon eat the sweetmeats ?" "Yes," said Ursula, boldly lying. She had heard Peggy lie to her little brother when it was necessary to keep him quiet for the sake of her mother. "And I'll put some poison in the sweetmeats. He'll eat 'em up, poison and all, and then he'll never do any harm no more."

The .poor invalid mother would have suffered agony if she could have heard this, her daughter, in- dulging in ungrammatical audacity. "You are not frightened?" she asked again, cuddling her brother, as soon as she had him safely outside the door-Abe two creeping stealthily through the garden for fear of Peggy. "No, not if you poison the dragon—you said you would ?" he answered, sturdily contending against scepticism. "Well, then,we'll enjoy ourselves out o' doors best time o' the day. It'll take a good while to get to the palace, but I'll carry you if you can't walk. And we'll creep in at the big gate just when the dragon can't see us. Perhaps he'll be having his tea, and then we'll make our way through the wood to the fairy. We will tell her our story, and she'll give us some of the gold she wears on her rich dresses, and —and—a talisman —that's what I think they call it —which you can slip inside your jacket, and it will make Peggy wonderful good to us when we come back. Stead of scolding she'll pet us." "Are you sure ?" Ursula 's own little heart was beating fast as she' nodded assent, dragging her brother after her, and making her way at running speed over the fields in the immediate neighbourhood of the village. In their haste and excitement the children took short cuts, not waiting to think of the young turnips or mangel-wurzel with which the brown earth was planted, and to which their trampling feet could do considerable mischief.

Somebody shouted to them, with the natural effect of making them run the faster, scrambling over hedges and through ditches, regardless of rents and scratches, in their hurry to reach the pretty lane where they would be hidden by the trees. "Are you sure," panted Ray, considerably out of breath. And Ursula whose morality was like that of most children' rather imitative than abstract, and who had noticed that Peggy in her mendacious statements to her little brother always stuck through thick and thin to her original declaration, though it might be what she called "a wopper' " answered nothing abashed, with a little toss of her head— Of course I am sure."

A quiet idyllic retreat in this fussy, agitated age was St. .Agatha's 'manor house. A survival of the earlier English civilisation—a haunt of poetry and dignity rather than of money-hunting, and pretence at grandeur. Altogether it belonged to a simpler and less complex life than ours. Long afterwards the recollection of it, as they saw it in that beautiful afternoon in May, was a restful memory, soothing to the imagination of Ursula Cam- pion. Her conscience gave her some pricks for her talk about poisoning the dragon' as she lay in ambush, some hours afterwards, with her little brother, rather _ _

like a dirty and ragged Pen, casting longing glances at the Gates of Paradise. She knew well enough that it was the lodge people taking their tea, and not the dragons vomiting smoke, when she and Ray hid themselves beneath the straggling boughs of some hawthorn bushes, and waited until the supposed poison, conveyed in a few sweetmeats flung close to the lodge, should take its supposed effect. Raymond had grown impatient as the afternoon drew on. She had given him nearly all the chocolates, and they weresuffenngfromtheunusual pangs of hun- ger as well as fatigue. She had even carried him, though he was nearly as big as herself, for a part of the way, and had cut her wrist badly in trying to climb a mall on which there were pieces of broken glass. But she bit her lips to keep down the pa in, as she put her arms round him and held him by main force, not daring to venture near enough to be seen till a woman came out from the lodge and left one of the gates ajar. Then was the opportunity for the children to creep in, entering into all the joys of the first man in his in- nocence. They spent the next hour in idling amongst the trees and flowers. But even Paradise palls on people who are suffering,from hunger. "Let us go and see the fairy, it must be time now," said Raymond pettishly, when his sister kept him dawdling longer than he had expected in the narrow walk between the hedges and clipped bcOE and yew. His feet were beginning to ache again, and he was tiring of the formality of the old English garden. "In a minute," said the little girl, who was suffering equal tortures from the unsatisfied pangs of her appetite, but whose heart began to misgive her as to the success of her enterprise, making her for a time the mere fearful of the two. No wonder that the details of that old-fashioned garden were afterwards stereotyped on her imagination. With one pretext or another she kept little Ray's hand tight in her's as they wandered over the wooden bridge, past the quadrangle of the Tudor period, to the adjacent chapel, in which so many had wor- shipped, and into which they peeped with curious eyes' catching glimpses of its carved pulpit, stalls, and old rood screen.

Ch Don't like it," whimpered lay with a little shiver. "I wants to go to the big house to see the fairy with the silver ' locks. Iso tired! I so hungry! Why don't the fairy come to us '1" and he stamped his foot in impotent rage. " Stoopid fairy " Ursula's heart gave a great leap as she looked in a scared way at the rounded summits Of the huge trees, beyond which she could see the turrets of the grandest part of the house, in which beyond a doubt'were the state apartments of the fairy. There was silence everywhere, and the shades of evening were already deepening on the trees. Mysteries and adventures were all very well in story-books; they were a little daunting when one was miles away from home in a strktnge country. She could have borne the pangs of her own hunger, but her pitiful sympathy for the little lad to whoin she had been accustomed to act the part of a sort of juvenile mother was more than she could endure. "No, she ain't a stoopid fairy. Just you keep close to me, and we'll go and fina her," said the child determinedly taking her courage in both her hands. She could never afterwards tell exactly how it happened. Probably .she fainted, owing to the loss of blood through the injury to her wrist. All she could remember was knocking at the excellently- moulded oak door, the nearest approach to the house from the quadrangle which antiquarians assigned to the Tudor period. "Take us to our fairy grandmother," she stammered out to the servant, who looked won- deringly and scornfully at the two shabbily dressed children,both more or less stained, not only with mud but with the drops of blood which now and then had been difficult to staunch. "Go away; we don't encourage beggars here," she said, trying to push the little girl back in her effort to close the door. Then the joint effects of unusual effort, combined with fatigue, hunger, and exhaustion, told on the naturally healthy constitution. "Ask our fairy grandmother to come herself," said the child, suddenly extending her arms, as if to keep herself from falling, then swaying and sinking un- conscious on the oak flooring of the old-fashioned hall. If her brother, who set up a portentous howl, had , not thrßwn himself in her way, so as to lessen the violence of the fall, the little girl would have struck her head. Howl after howl rang through the quiet house, each one more protracted and agonising than the last. It was enough to wake any amount of ghosts, as the servant observed. But the result was still more astonishing to the children. .

When Ursula opened her eyes again she was no longer in the hall, but in a handsoffie room, the sight of which was awe-inspiring. The sombre colouring of the oakpanelled walls, with hangings of tapestry over the doors, and the dark timbers of the ceiling undisfigured by the vandalism of modem plaster, would have recalled to anyone but a child the almost mythic times of England's prime. There was a modesty of proportion perfect in itself. Nothing was exaggerated or on the palatial scale, nothing vulgarly ostentatious. The heavy mullioned windows had no adornment but that of dark velvet curtains, and in the china-tiled fireplace logs of wood smoul- dered, for though it was the month of May the evenings were still chilly. The room itself struck the child as the fulfilment of a dream. The background of the picture was not so amazing as the figure which bent over her—that of an old lady with silver hair, and great sapphires and shining diamonds on her fingers. If her ciress had no gold stars on it, it was trimmed with magnificent lace, which Ursula could only wonder at without guessing its value. The lady's face was very pale, and her eyes shone as much as her. diamonds. The wonder was that these were as the eyes of Ursula's mother—eyes of the colour of wild hyacinths, fringed with black lashes, which were repeated in the case of little Ray. Nit neither Ray's eyes nor 'Mrs. Campion's were so startling as these, partly because the arched black brows and long lashes contrasted vividly with the silver hair, and partly because there was a pierc- ing look in these eyes, difficult to reconcile with ad- vanced age, and a aeep fold between the brows caused by worry or sorrow. The voice, too, was hard, metallic, and some- what strained, as if with an effort to keep emotion out of it. .

The room seemed to go round again, the spindle. legged chairs began to stand like acrobats on their heads, the floor advanced to meet the ceiling, the ceiling came down to meet the floor, as the child in- voluntarily closed her eyes, listening to the harsh tones of that voice. " It is all in-keeping with that fellow's underhand ways—a skilfully laid plot planned to take me in. No, Rogers, it is no use to talk to me; don't I know my own son-in-law to be as depraved a blackguard,, as arrant a knave, as is met with in the three king- doms. Think of the letter, which he skilfully unclosed and then closed again. Don't tell me the boy is like me. A boy of his will inherit all his failings; there is perhaps more hope of the girl, but—" The Voice had softened a little, and Ursula, who in her half-swooning condition had been unable to under- stand the conversation,took advantage of the change of tone to open her own good honest hazel eyes, and murmur vaguely,— " Oh have pity on little Ray! You are our beauti- ful fairy grandmother." ' Flattery of this unconscious sort is seldom unpleas- ing to women—.the more so when it is utterly unex- pected, arid is given at a time of life when the charm of beauty is said to be past. The old lady's lips twitched; there were soft little depressions on each side of the mouth,where once the dimples had played on her youthful cheeks. But she did not allow herself to relax her habitual sternness. It could scarcely be called a smile with which she said to her Attendant, "Tat, tut—more nonsence ; the poor child is to be pitied. With a father who believes in neither God nor devil, and an old fool of g nurse who has as many. superstitions as there are days in the year, I don't exp-ftt she has had any better training than a heathen." Here Ursula's spirit rose—the more so that little Ray, who had fallen asleep after being fed with hot soup, and soothed in the housekeeper's arms, woke and, frightened at the , strange faces, began to sob pitifully for his mammy. "Give him to me," said the little girl, making another of the efforts which had already cbst her so much, and staggering to her feet. It was my fault—all my fault—to bring him here to his fairy , grandmother—beautiful to look at as they say in the fairy books, but white as snow, and cold as ice." She was interlarding her talk, as she often did, with quotations from one of her fairy tales, and did not watch to _notice the effect of her words.

_ She saw only little Ray, and in another moment she had her brother tenderly in her arms in spite ol the wrist which had been carefully bandaged,and in spite of the cold water whith they had thrown on her little face, and which was falling in great drops from her golden-red hair. " Never mind, my darling," she said, as she cooed to him in such a voice as that in which the stock.

dove coos to its young. "Never mind—we'll go back to rnammy—and if Peggy is a little cross we 11 never look no more for any fairy grandmothers." The sight of the womanly little face bent over another nearly as big as itself, and of the effort the girl was making to forget her own troubles and think only of her brother would hasp touched many hearts. Ray had ceased to sob, but the big tears were coursing each other down Mrs. Maclurchan's cheeks. "It is too much for me, Rogers; at my age one cannot stand these strong emotions, and I have no doubt that my son-in-law counted on this. It is like him to be always hatching up plots, but he won't find that this one will succeed,"—she added, raising her voice. "No, let the girl understand my message—l give it once and for all. No son of has shall ever be 'heir to my property. I can leave it as I will. No Campion shall ever inherit—no,not though the boy has violets for his eyes as they once said. I had for mine. Let him be ever so much like his mother, that mother deceived me, and I can never for- give deception." She had walked across the room as she said this, with much dignity of carriage, as few wom*a walk in the present generation. She straightened her back as she reached the door-- there were still eloquent lines in that back telling of pride of character. By this time she had re- covered herself, and looked once more at the children and at Rogers, who shewed as much feeling under the circumstances as she dared show consistently with her vocation as a well-trained machine. "Yes, it is a pretty tableau," she said bitterly as she halted. "All the more effective on account of the rags and dirt. Pity they can't shew it off at one of the London theatres. It would supply Campion with money for absinthe, with whin, as surely as there is a God above us, / will never supply him. That man always kept company with strolling players, but he must try his histrionics on some one else. Wash the children, Rogers, and feed them well. To-morrow they shall be sent back to their home in the carriage. And then she continued, as i she had forgotten the presence of her attendant, and was speaking half-musingly—as the old do some- times—to herself, "I wonder who the girl is like. 'Ph AV have Riven her my name—more's the

div.head: AN EXTRAORDINARY CHARGE.
div.p: AN EXTRAORDINARY CHARGE.

Before Mr. W. Pilkington and Dr. E. P. Twyford, I at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Ambrose Walter Winstanlay, ef 88, North-read, st. Helens. an assistant ironmonger, at Liverpool, was sum- moned by the London and North-Western Railway Company, on a charge of annoying a lady passenger in a train between Huyton and Huyton Quarry, on the Bth June. Defendant, who was represented by Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens, pleaded not guilty.— Mr. Preston, who prosecuted, stated that the offence with which the prisoner was charged was one of behaving indecently in a railway carriage. On the night, of the date in question, four passengers were in a carriage of a train leaving Lime-st., and go- ing in the direction of St. Helens. One was the defendant, and another was a girl whom he would call to give evidence. The othqr two left the train, at Broad Green Station, and shortly afterwards the prisoner went and sit opposite to her. He talked about the weather for some time, and shortly after, the,train left Huyton he disarranged his clothing. At that moment the train stopped at Huyton Quarry, and the girl jumped out and ran to the guard, cal- ling attentioh to the defendant's conduct. She was eventually got into another compartment and was taken on to her destination. The Company thought they were justified in bringing that charge of inter- fering with the comfort of a passenger, although there might have been another charge laid under the Vagrancy Act.—Elizabeth Mann, a widow, lately cook in the service of Mrs. Anderson, Rain- hill, and at present residing at 40, James-st., Wiol- nes, then gave evidence in support of Mr. Preston's stateraent.—ln reply to questions, witness said the defendant never made any attempt to touch or seize her.—William Bettony, guard of the train, gave evidence as to the complaint. He went to the defendant in the train, and the defendant said it was entirely a mistake.—Railway-inspector Standford spoke to seeing the defendant and telling him of the charge. He denied having behaved im- properly in any way.—For the defence, Mr. Swift said he did not think, on the evidence before them, the Bench would be disposed to properly and safely convict the defendant on the charge against him. He thought it was one of the strangest stories ever told in that court. He referred to the respecta- bility of the defendant and his parents, and said he held in hia hands testimonials as to the defendant's character from all sorts and conditions of men. He asked the magistrates could they believe the story? —At this point the Chairman interrupted Mr. Swift, and said the Bench were not disposed to convict the defendant, and the summons would be dis- missed.

div.head: FROM LONDON LETTER,
div.p: FROM LONDON LETTER,

Toboganners should beware. A gentleman at the Irish Exhibition was relieved of his watch, purse, and other valuables by a comely lady who asked him, with a winning smile on starting, to allow her to calm her apprehensions by clasping him round the waist during the descent. Lord Colin Campbell is, I hear, going out to India in the autumn to practice as a barrister in the Bom- bay High Court. If he does as well as the Bombay barrister who appeared for the notorious Sirdar Diler Jung at the Parliamentary inquiry into the Deccan mining concession, Lord Colin will not regret his change of residence. The counsel in question is reputed to make an income of from £lO,OOO to £12,000 a year. A fashion of wearing a glove of different colour on either 1 'ome into vogue in France, and the story ( 7oduction runs that a certain charming Lr duchess had promised to be present at i for a charitable object in the Casino at Ti Being rather late in starting, she took her gloves to put on in the carriage, and did not notice that she had taken up one white and one black glove from the two pairs laid out by her mild. As her dress was of black and white silk, everyone thought that it was the latest chic, and it passed into popular adoption at Trouville. It is considered probable that the Local Govern- ment Bill will be sent up to the Lords about the be- ginning of next month. Some of the peers are by no means pleased at hating to sit through the early part of August to discuss the measure, because they cannot, with any show of decency, hurry through its consideration; arid, with all the excisions, it re- mains a formidable bill. 14; consists of 122 clauses and three schedules, and in its printed form covers 106 folio pages. Sir John Simon has given notice of an amend- ment excluding th e defendants in the case of O'Donnell v.Walter and Another from the benefit of th 3 indem- nity clause. Mr. Labouchere has also intimated that he will propose an addition to the indemnity clause providing that nothing in it shall relieve the authors, printers, and publishers of any libel pub- lished before the passing of the Act from any civil or criminal liability. Mr. E. Robertson intends also to propose that it shall not be competent for any law officer of the Crown to appear for any parties before the- commission.

I am glad to hear that Sir Charles Bowen, who is on the whole the best judge on the English bench, declares himself highly satisfied with the composi- tion of the Judicial Commission. Sir James Han- nen is certainly a model jtAlge— dignified, resolute, and very acute. Mr. Justice Smith is conspicuous for strong sense anti manly force. The weak point of the Commission would seem to be the selection of Mr. Justice Day, who, like all English Roman Catholics, is strongly opposed to his Irish co-reli- gionists on the subject of Home Rule. No one, however, entertains the slightest doubt of his es- sential impartiality.

The season dies hard. Lady Rothschild's party on Wednesday night was one of the brightest and plea- santest of the summer. It was intended as in some measure a substitute for the great ball which was to have been given for the Prince and Princess of Wales, but had to be abandoned on account of the Emperor Frederick's death. Among the guests on Wednesday night were Lord Rothschild s sister, Baroness Alphonse de Rothschild, wife of the head of the Paris house, and the Princesse de Wagram, sister of Lady Rothschild. To the great delight of many friends, Lady Rosebery appeared at her cousin's party, quite recovered from her recent illness. There was some delicious music, and Sarah Bernhardt gave some recitations, among them her favourite little piece, "Les Deux Pigeons." From Lord Rothschild's many of the guests went onto the Duchess of Buccleuch's ball in Montagu House.

Mr. T. O'Kelly, M.P. for North Roscommon. who was arrested in Mark-lane, has had a remarkable and adventurous career. He was educated at the Uni- versity of Dublin and at the Sorbonne, Paris. For some time he served in the French Army, taking part in the Franco-German War, and retiring as captain after the fall of Paris. lie then became a journalist, and was for a while one of the editors of the " New York Herald." As newspaper corres- pondent he went to Cuba. In that capacity he visited Cespedes and the Cuban rebels. On return- ing to the Spanishlines he was arrested, tried, and sentenced to death. He was, howeyer, saved by Senor Castlelar, and wrote an account of his adven- tures. In 1876 he took part in the expedition against the Sioux chief Sitting Bull, and in 1884 he went to the Soudan with the intention of visiting the Malidi. His intention was, however, frustrated, as he was stoppedtat Gongola by order of the Egyp- tian Government.

At Mr. Gladstone's wedding, on the 26th of July, 1839, Sir Francis oyle was the best man, and he has left us. both ir prose and verse, some account of the happy event. "in 1839," he writes in his Reminiscences, "P attended Mr. Gladstone's wed- ding at Hawarden as his best man. Catherine Glynne and her sister Mary, both beautiful women, were married on the same day, the first to William Gladstone. the second to George, Lord Lvttelton. The occasion was a very interestingr one from the high character of the two bridegrooms tied the warmth of affection felt for the two charming young ladies by all their friends and neighbours in every rank of life. There was a depth and genuine- ness of sympaty diffused around which, as the French say, spoke for itself without any words." I Such is the narrative in prose. The poetical narra- tive will be found in a poem published in a volume of miscellaneous verses, and entitled "To two sister brides who were married on the same day." We hear of the invention of a new game which is to supersede the hackneyed lawn tennis and cro- quet, told give ladies the opportunity of displaying their elegance of attitude. "Keep your eye on that of your partner" is the first rule laid down. Surely there must be a favourable result. The new- fashioned dresses, with tight aprons in front and saddle bags behind, will be admirably adapted to the occasion. The game can be played under cover, without bats or battledores, and is a more refined and complicated game of ball, wherein the lady and gentleman each try the other's skill more than either agility or pOwer. The new game has been started by the Badmintons. No name is given to it as yet, and the grave question as to whose name it is to bear has beer i the occasion of some lively dis- puting among the members of the club assembled for the express purpose of solving the difficulty. So the girls are beginning to practice the art and mys- ' tery of the new game according to the rules laid ' down—and to work hard with renewed hope and vigour.

Lord Wolverton's will is, says the "Star," in- valid. For someNme there have been rumours to that effect, but they have not generally been be- lieved, but thereis no further room for doubting their accuracy. The whole of the immense fortune passed from the kresent Lord Wolverton to a colla- teral branch. It%ppears that the will of the second baron, who was so well known as the Liberal Whip andPostmaster-General, was drawn up inaccurately. He undoubtedly intended that the personal estate, which amounts to more than £3,000,000, should go with the title, hot the will was so worded that in- stead of devolving on the present lord, who is the brother of the third baron, the personalty returns to the brother of the second baron. This unfor- tunate mistake on the part of the lawyers is piece of bad luck for the Liberal party, as the present Lord Wolverton is a. staunch Home Ruler and a genuine Liberal. It was fully anticipated that he would follow the example of his uncle, and devote a portion of his wealth to the political party in whose principles he is such a firm believer.

div.head: PERSONAL.
div.p: PERSONAL.

Lord Cams called attention to the letter written by Sir William Harcourt to Mr. Herbert Gladstone, con- taining extracts from the biography of the late Mr. For. star. In the course of one of the entrants it was stated that "Sir R. Cross, on the part of the official Con- servatives, had notified his intention to move as an amendment to Sir John Hay's motion a resolution in favour of the immediate release of Mr. Parnell and his fellow members. Ministers who had been abused with such vehemence a few weeks before because they were supposed to he dealing with the Nationalist party in Ire- land with criminal leniency, now found that the Tory party was the first to attack them on the opposite ground." Lord Cross proceeded to explain that the notice of amendment referred to emanated from the late Mr. Rynaston Cross, then the LibPral member for Bolton. The argument founded on the erroneous assumption in consequence fell to the ground. In reply to Lord Greville, Earl CADOGAN said it would be premature to promise any legislation next session in the direction of the purchase of Irish railways by the Itovemment. The Patents, Designs, and Trades Marks Bill passed its third reading.—Other legislation having been dealt with, their lordships adjourned at 5 25.

div.head: ROUSE OF COMMONS.-MONDAY.
div.p: ROUSE OF COMMONS.-MONDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at 3 5 p.m. A number of private bills were advanced a stage, in • eluding the Manchester, Sheffield. and Lincolnshire New Railway Bill, the North Cornwall and Plymouth. Devonport, and South-West Junction Railway Bill, and the Staffordshire Potteries Water Bill. Mr. PLIINKET refused to enter into communication with the Duke of Cambridge in view of the retention of Wimbledon for the annual shooting competitions of the volunteers. A question stood on the paper in the ra-ne of Mr. Conybeare, and the Speaker inadvertently called upon the hon. gentleman, who, of course, being suspended, was not in his place. The incident evoked some cheering from the Irish benches. Mr. Sierra intimated that no restriction of the im- portation of cheap sugar into this country could be effected without the consent of Parliament. He could not vet state what action the Government would take in r( .erence to the sugar bounties convention.

div.head: SUPPLY.
div.p: SUPPLY.

After the questions -h-aa- -Con-eluded, the Report of Supply was taken, and upon the vote for the Colonial Office, Dr. (lenity, moved a resolution in order to criti- cise the Government policy in Zululand. He urged the desirability of having a commission to inquire into the condition of things in South Africa. Sir J. GOREY thought neither the present Government nor preceding Governments which had administered the affairs of Zululand deserved the wholesale censure passed by the hon. member. He contended that the present Government of the country was sound, and that the policy her Majesty's Government were following de- served the confidence of the House. The reinforcements sent out would direct their action against Dinizulu, and the Government had no wish to visit tha Basutos with any severity. It was, however, impossible to tolerate the presence in Zululand of the rebel eiiefs. Mr. Osborne Morgan and Sir G. Baden-Powell having contributed to the discussion, Mr. Jour; MORLEY referred to our mistakes in Zulu- land having arisen from not regarding the national spirit among the Zulus. In the present case the people we were fighting were the majority of the natives, and in spite of our experience we were going to pursue the same policy that had led to former disasters. In Mr. r.7HAMBERLATN Dinizulu found a friend, and the right hon. gentleman further expressed an opinion that many of our difficulties in South Africa arose from an erroneous interpretation of the situation by those in authority. Mr. STANTIOPR believed there would be no friction be- tween the High Commissioner and the officer in command. The report on the vote was agreed to.
THE PARNELL COMMISSION.
NAMES OF THE JUDGES.-SPEECH OF MR, GLAD- STONE.

Mr. W. N. Sstrrn moved the second reading of the Charges and Allegations Bill. He said if the inquiry was to be of use it must be complete and searching, and he had confidence in the tribunal which was proposed. The Government named Sir James Ilannen as president of the Commission, with Mr. Justice Day and Mr. Jus- tice Smith.

Mr. Pantreu- said it was against the Land League and not against himself that this trial was being issued. Much of the speech of the Attorney-General was without foundation, and the rest of it was without sense. He objected to the wide terms of the bill, which would enable the commission to inquire into every speech delivered and every outrage committed in Ireland before coming to the question of the forged letters. It was un-English. cowardly, and unjust to ask them to accept such a commission In response to their ehatlenee for a committee to inquire into the authenti- city' of the forged letters. There was nothing new ex- cept those letters in the charges made against him per- sonally, which were matters of public notoriety. Fie called upon the Government to limit the inquiry to the charges made against himself and members of Parlia- ment, and not to include other persons. He also called upon them to name the members implicated, to state the specific charges against them, to secure that the in- quiry should be conducted judicially, and that the docu- ments should be called for at the outset, so that the parties concerned might have the opportunity of examin- ing them.

Mr. GLADSTONE made one or two attempts to rise, hesitating each time. At last, seeing that no one else rose to speak, he got up, amid loud Opposition cheers. He expressed his astonishment that, after the plain and expressed demands Mr. Parnell made upon the Govern- ment in respect to inquiry on the speech of counsel in the case of O'Donnell v. The Times, no answer had been made. (Opposition cheers.) It was out of their power to make the Government speak if they found it expedi- ent to keep their mouths shut. (Laughter.) Speak- ing for his section of the House, he said their position was one of less responsibility than any other portion. Last session they explained their view, that by justice, by policy, by precedent, by regard to the jurisdiction uniformly assumed by the House over its own members, in cases where their public character was gravely impugned, the House was bound to appoint a Select Committee to make the inquiry. (Cheers.) Mr. Smith had deliberately given his opinion against that method of proceeding, and said—and this indicated the general poverty of his case—that he relied as a precedent upon the Commission of Inquiry into the charges against the Metropolitan Board of Works. (Rear.) mit the Metropolitan Board WAS not a section of the House, ad they could not deal w'th the members of the Board. Mr. Smith said since last year the position of the twee. lion had been totally altered. How had it been altered? By a speech of counsel not supported by a rag of evidence. New letters had been produced, but they fell into the same category as the letters last year. In making the speech the Attorney-General must have been instructed by one of the parties, and it added nothing whatever in weight, power, or authority to the original allegations. (Opposition cheers.) The right hon. gentleman had given us the names of three judges to constitute the tribunal. Mr. Gladstone did not retract what he had said with respect to the general character of the Bench, but it was in the power of the right hon. gentleman to *have made a selection which would at once have hushed every mouth. fie could not say with respect to the whole of those three names that he had made such a selection. ("Oh," and cheers.) Mr. Parnell asked that the proceeding should be a judicial proceeding. That could not raise any difficulty. Mr. Smith must feel that they should make such reasonab!e provisions as might clearly declare the mind of Parliament in regard to the nature and limits of this heavy task. They were devolving upon others a responsibility which belonged to themselves— (Opposition cheers),—and therefore should make dear the lines on which the substitutes were to work. The next article laid down by the hoq, member for Cork was that the words "other persons" be excluded from the bill. (Cheers.) He never saw anything with greater aston- ishment than those words. Mr. Swam : I mertionecl other persons when 1 Made my statement. on Thursday and put in the paper On Friday. At all events it was always in my mind. MT. GLADSTONE continued Was it seriously contended that they were going to appoint a committee of inquiry into the acts of other persons, subjects of her Majesty, who were not distinctly before them in an capacity whatever, with regard to whom no definite allegations had been made, and who might include any number of thousands of her Majesty's subjects. The whole ground of proceeding did not seem to have been understood by the Government. It rested upon the historical and constitutional fact that the House assumed juris- diction over the conduct of its own members in mat- ters of public vitality affecting their capacity to serve the public in the House That was the reason, if there be a reason, for the inquiry. The fetters alleged were of a character that evidently if they were proved to be genuine would require such notice o? the House as he should not describe. The members of Parliament who were to be the object of the inquiry—necessarily one with a penal aspect—were bound tq be pointed out as the subjects of the charge. (Cheers.) Gentlemen who might possibly have a share in the imputations were entitled to claim that they should be brought out in the light of day, so that there should be some responsibility in making these terrific charges and people should not be able to recede' from them by saying "It was not you whom I meant"— (Parnellite cheers),--" it %vas somebody else, whom I have named," and in that case they provide a shelter and a refuge for a skulking cowardice of Such baseness as no words could adequately describe. He wished to learn from the Government whether they intended to defend the charges that were to be the subject of inves- tigation. There were but two. First and foremost came the letters alleged to be forged. These were the

'bad and front :of the matter. (Cheers.) Every. thing else passed the ordeal of their debate frow 1880 to 1885, passed the ordeal of dissolution of 1885. (cheers)—passed the ordeal of the Tory policy of that memorable autumn which history could never forget— (Opposition cheere)—of the ordeal of the general election, without raising a single scruple in the minds of the then Ministers of the Crown, whose duty it was, if they thought there was a ease, to make the inquiry and bring these evils deeds to light. There was that charge of the forgery of the letters, and the question whether any member of the ,House was guilty of complicity ir crime. That was a charge he had never made: no coller.^:ie of his had ever made; it WW a charge - should not have scrupled to make if they h• d there was anything to sup:ort it. Mr Gladstone finally maintained that the charges should be specified, that the persons should be named, and that the inquiry should be confined to members of the House. Unless these concessions were made he would not have any responsibility for the bill, and, as at present advised, he declined to express any confidence'in the composition of the Commission. He agreed with Mr. Parnell that the letters were the pivot on which the whole matter turned, and he regarded the Attorney-General's accept- ance of The Times brief as deplorable. The HOME SECRETARY defended' the action of the Attorney-General in appearing as counsel for The rases, and repudiated the idea that the Government had in any sense made themselves parties to the charges and alle- gations. The whole substance of the charges was that certain persons, some members of Parliament and some not, were involved in complicity with crime, in con- nivance with crime, and in association with criminals. That was the charge, and if the House struck out "Other persons," away went all inquiry into the doings of the flan-na-Gael, and they would reduce the inquiry to a farce. .

• CYIARTALS RCWIELL. knowing something of actions! for libel, would infinitely prefer an action for libel before the most bigoted and partisan jury in the City of Lon- don than the tribunal constituted on the unfair and dis- advantageous terms in this bill. He -remarked upon the unfairness of inquiring into criminal charges not definitely specified, and complained of the action of The Ttmes in pleading that the allegations in " Parnel- ham and Crime" did not apply to Mr. O'Donnell and then immediately repeating them against Mr. Parnell and other members of the Irish Parliamentary party. The SOLICITOR-GENERAL taunted the Opposition with inconsistency in their speeches against the bill, and spoke of Sir Charles Russell as the unavowed adviser for the plaintiff in the recent action. Mr. T. P. O'CONNOR reproached the Government for framing the bill in consultation with the Attorney- General, and insisted that the letters ascribed to Mr. Parnell afforded ample ground for inquiry without any of the other issues proposed to be brought within its scope. The Irish members were eager for an inquiry into their conduct, but they objected to have mixed up with it, an investigation into the action of a tolitical organisation. He would concede that Byrne and Ford were guilty of crime, but what the Government and The Times had to prove was complicity on the part of the Irish members. _ _

Mr. LABODCITERg moved the adjournment of the de- bate, which Mr. AV. B. SM!TIT opposed as being contrary to understanding in the H0,15P on the ~,` Lanoommas ‘vithdrew his motirn. in speaking against the Nil at 12 o'clock, when the,. • stood ad- journed.—Mr. W. FL SUITTI proposed to resume the debate next day, and hoped it would be concluded before dinner. .
After scme further business had been transacted, the House adjourned at 12 20. _ HOUSE OF LORDS.--TuEsnev. _

The House assembled at four p.m. Bitts PASSED.—The Royal Assent was given to a number of public and private bills, including the Man. chester Ship Canal (No. 1) Bill, the Habitual Drunkards Amendment Act Bill, and the London Seawater Supply Bill. The Commissioner, were the Lord Chancellor, the Earl of Lathoin, and the Earl of Kintore. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4 15 p.m. The Manchester Ship Canal (No. 2) Bill was read a third time.

Werrnaram expwsed his anxiety for`inquiry into the charges, but pointed out that the House had already refused the inquiry for which alone there was precedent. What could be thought of the conduct of the proprietor or editor of 771 e Times who, having in his possession letters making the most serious accusations, waited till a convenient opportunity for their production, as if the letters were so many old curiosities, the market value of which might vary? (Opposition cheers.)

Mr. CHAMI3ERLAIN said as the letters must form the principal feature of the inquiry, he thought it should be left to the judges to determine how these should be in- quired into. But he objected to any limitation, as it must hamper or limit inquiry into the truth. The limi- tations proposed by Mr. Parnell might shield those who were guilty simply because they might be members of Parliament. If the charge against the member for Cork were a criminal charge he should say to the Govern- ment, why do you not prosecute him? But it was not a criminal charge. He appealed to the lawyers of the House whether it was not a charge of moral com- plicity which involved moral guilt rather than a charge of an actual criminal offence. In that case there was no possibility of the hon. member clear- ing himself of the charge unless he was allowed to go into his connection with other persons. He thought the inquiry was one which the hon. members below the gangway ought to accept. It was the fullest, freest, most complete investigation into the whole circum- stances. No attempt to limit the inquiry, even though it should be thought a waste of time or of money, should stop it a minute. The Bill was presented to hon. mem- bers, especially the hon. member for Cork, for them to reject or accept as they thought fit. The hon. member, he understood, rejected it. That being so, the Govern- ment might well consider their position. They could with perfect consistency withdraw the Bill, but he yen- tured to say that the matter was really now out of their hands. It was in the hands of the House of Commons, and it was for the honour and dignity of the House of Commons that the whole matter should be inquired into. _ .

Sir W. Ilencounr objected to this political prosecution, and declared that when he was in office with Lord Spen- cer they never discovered any evidence whicn would connect Mr. Parnell or any of the Irish representatives with complicity in or the perpetration of crime. The SOLICITOR-GBNEEIAL for SCOTLAND defended the action of the Government. The inquiry was now a ques- tion affecting the State, which must know the associa- tion or connection of a political party with the grosser forms of crime. The question really before the House was whether, having constituted a legal tribunal, they were to give It the powers possessed by similarly con- stituted commissions. Mr. T. M. HEALY said he declined to submit to a "fish- ing inquiry." Mr. BALLANTYNE thought the right course was a prose- cution, and not a commission. The debate was continued by Mr Lockwood, Mr Dar- ling, Sir John Simon, Mr Hunter, Mr Finlay, Mr E Robertson, and the Attorney-General, after which the Bill was read a second time without a division. RAILWAY BILL.—One of the principal features of the business was the consideration of the Railway and Canal Traffic Bill. The first point raised in the debate was by Sir G. CAMPBELL, who complained of the absence in the measure of provision with regard to passenger traffic and for remedying the grievances of small traders.—The PRESIDENT of the BOARD of TRADE disposed of this by re- minding hon. members that he was under a pledge to consider the question of public safety at the earliest pos- sible moment.—Mr. MuNnxt.tx spoke of the progress of the bill in Grand Committee as having given a great im- pulse to the principle of delegation.—After an amend- ment had been agreed to as to the hearing of railway cases by the Commission, there came a somewhat pro- tracted discussion on an amendment by Mr. JAMES STEVENSON in favour of the retention of the power to grant preferential rates, the contention of the hon. mem- ber for South Shields being met by the assertion of Sir M. HICKS-BEACH that the bill only secured equal treat- ment for home and foreign produce and was a fair coin- promise.—To this Mr. MUNDELLA and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said ditto emphatically, and the clause was negatived without a division, the bill being afterwards read a third time. NATIONAL DEFENCE.—The House, proceeding to the consideration of the National Defence Bill, found that clause 2 of that measure gave some anxiety to Sir Ed. Hamlev, who regarded it as practically an application of the Militia Act to the volunteer. Although no doubt the idea would be groundless, it would be thought that the volunteers were to take the place of the militia, and the ranks of the former forcewould sufferinconsequence. —Some difference of opinion was expressed by Colonel Laurie and Mr. Howard Vincent, who immediately fol- lowed; and Colonel BLuNDELL, while thinking that the hon. member for Birkenhead had rather exaggerated the case, made a point of a declaration by the War Office being given that the volunteers were only to be called out in case of emergency. Mr. Molloy and Mr. Row- lands were among the opponents of the clause because they saw in it a veiled movement in the direction of com- pulsory military service. Others including Mr. Brunner and Mr. W. M•Laren, were hostile to it because of the possible difficulties to which it might give rise between employers and employed; and while Mr. BRODERICK stated that the proposal appeared to be generally re- garded as one to improve the machinery of mobilisation and not to increase the liabilities of volunteers, Sir GEORGE TREVELYAN feared its effect would be to make the volunteers a divided force. The discussion resulted in no definite conclusion being arrived at, the proceed- ings in Committee being adjourned - • -

- - QuEsTioNs, &c.—After the Attorney-General had in reply to Sir W. Houldsworth made an admission of the importance of the question *affecting the rating of machinery, which admission was not, however, as the hon. Baronet desired, accompanied by a promise of legis- lation on the subject next session, the SPEAKER announced that he had received a letter from Sir J. Ingham, metropolitan magistrate, containing the information of the arrest of Mr. James O'Kelly in the city.—This naturally gave rise to questions from the Irish party, Mr. PARNELL leading off with a demand to be informed whether the hon. member could not have been cited be- fore an Irish court of summary jurisdiction, without being placed under arrest.—Mr. SEXTON, who described the mode of proceeding in the case as cowardly and vin- dictive, asked whether Mr. O'Kelly would be allowed bail.—To the Irish leader's question the Solicitor- General for Ireland gave no decided answer ; but the CHIEF SECRETARY did take up the matter of bail after be- ing two or three times approached on the point, and said that it would not be refused except on very good grounds.—The House next listened to Mr. Borrcrittny Fiala disclaiming any responsibility for an interruption which he was reported to have caused while the Attorney- General was speaking on the previous night, and then adjourned at five minutes to six o'clock.

div.head: LIBEL LAWS.
div.p: THE LIBEL LAWS.

The House went into Committee upon the Libel Law Amendment Bill. On Clause 4, Lord MONILSIVELL, who had charge of the bill, moved the introduction of the words bona fide be- t ween "a" and "public meeting." The amendment had, lie said, been introduced at the suggestion of the National Association of Journalists.—The LORD CHANCELLOR said he found a difficulty in determining what was a public meeting in the legal sense of the term.--,Lord ilauscntra. defined it as a meeting for public purposes. —The amendment was agreed to. It was also decided to introduce into the same clause the words, "whether the admission to the meeting be general or restricted, unless where the proceedings art- declared to he private by resolution." Further on, all the words after " not " were taken out, and " publishe,i in the public interest" inserted. Clause 5, which provides for the consolidation of actions brought against several defendants, was allowed to stand. Lord COLERTDGE moved the insertion of the following new clause:—" Section 3, of 44th and 45th Viet., cap. 60. is hereby repealed, and instead thereof be it enanteti that no criminal prosecution shall be commenced against any proprietor, publisher, editor, or any person respon- sible for the publication of any newspaper, or other publication, for any libel published therein withote written fiat of her Majesty's Attorney-General in Eng- land and Ireland respectively, or without the order of a Judge at Chambers being first heard and ob- tained ; application for such fiat, allowance, or order being made either to the Attorney-General or to the judge aforesaid, but not to both; that such application shall be made on notice to the person accused, who shall have an opportunity of being heard against such application." The noble and learned tort said that under the present system the fiat of the Public Prosecutor was obtained almost as a matter of course In the Wood v. Cox case, he had received a statement from a number of newspaper proprietors, who were re. :pert-able persons, on the subject. He thought the function of turning a civil cause of action into a crimine I ttroeeedine should be exercised by a person responsibl • to the public. The LORD CHANCELLOR objected to any other public-1- tion being included in the same category as an ordinary newspaper. He did not object to the function of grant- ing the fiat resting with the Attorney-General. Lord BERSCRELL could not regard a libel which affected a mnn's character as being the same as an ordinary cause of action. He did dot object to the clause which had been proposed although he did not attach much itnnortance to it. Lord CotEatnox considered that a crime should be something in which the public were interested. H. would not oppose the striking out of the words "or other publication." This having been done, the clause was agreed to. The further consideration of the measure wan postponed. -
The House adjourned at 620. . . HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Tunney.

The Speaker took the chair at 3 p.m. Mr. JOTIN Ruts moved for a copy of rules and regula. tions in force in the prisons in Ireland. Mr. HOWARD VINCENT raised the subject of trade strikes, and was informed by the PRESIDENT of the HOARD Of TRADE that there were last year 26 strikes re- corded in the United Kingdom. 15 of which were unsoc- cessful, 10 Successful; while one was undecided. The right hon. gentleman did not think public opinion was ripe for the introduction of a system of State arbitration snob as existed in the United states. Several Radical and Irish members endeavoured to in- duce the Irish Secretary to give facilities for the dis- cussion of the Irish Drainage Bills before 12 o'clock, but without success. Thereupon Mr. MACDONALD excitedly exclaimed, "It is monstrous." and Dr. HUNTER deelarell his intention of following up Mr. Conybeare's intention of dividing the Rouse against the bills. Mr. ANDERSON sought to ascertain whether it was Ln• the direct instructions of the Government that the late Mr. Mandeville was forcibly stripped of his clothes in TuDamore Gaol.-Mr. BALFOUR. however, merely replied that the question of prison rules was no* before the coroner.
