He entirely objected to the proposed Commission of judges. A Committee of the House was the proper body to investigate these charges against members of the House. United Ireland was at least as respectable as The Tinies—(laughter)—and they had just as much right to call upon the Irish Secretary. constantly attacked a-, he was by United Ireland:. to go before an Irish jury as the Government had to call upon the Irish members to go before a Middlesex jury. The right hon. gentleman had moreover libelled an Irish member—(laughter)-- and had run away. (Renewed laughter.) At this juncture, Black llod smeared at the door of the House. The usual warning call was, however, drowned in the general la it•hter. and so astonished was the hon. member by the sudden approach of the Lord's official, and the Speaker's constant call to order, that he resumed his Seat in such haste as to seriously crush his hat in the process, amid laughter from all parts of the House.—On the return of the Speaker, it was announced that the Royal Assent had been given to the Inebriates Act and other Acts. _

LABOUCITERE, resuming, asked would The Timms produce the name ot the forger of these letters?, The Attorney-General had said The Times would rather lose the verdict than do so. Did The Times adhere to the determination? IF so, the House should not grant a Com- mission which could not possibly go to the root of the question, and must be a humbua and delusion. The object of the Commission was really only to give Tie Times loaded dice with which to play this game—(lrish cheers)—and to divert the right attention from what was going on in Ireland now at the instance of the Government—(renewed cheers)—from the affair at Mitchelstown, from the horrible death of Mr. Mandeville —(cheers)—and from oth.r disgraceful events. For his part, yielding to the wish of Mr. Parnell he would not move his amendment to defeat the bill.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after four o'clock. Law OF LIBEL BILL.—The consideration of the Libel Law Amendment Bill was resumed in Committee, through which the measure passed, after Lord MONKS- WELL had intimated that it was his intention at a sub- sequent stage to bring up a clause which would render liable to prosecution the utterer of a libel at a public meeting, although the report of such meeting published in a newspaper would be privileged.—The Companies Bill also passed through Committee after various amendments, including two relating to dealing in shares before allotment, and. the qualifications of di- rectors with regard to shares,—Their lordships adjourned at 7-20. The National Defences, Excise Duties, and the Collection of Tithes Bills were-proposed to come on before the adjournment, and for tloe Sunday Closing Bill he would endeavour to set apaq a -morning sitting if Mr. I Stevenson Was not willing for it to go over until the autumn. div.head: VOLUNTEER CYCLIST MANCEUVRES. "ABANDONING WARRINGTON."
div.p: THE VOLUNTEER CYCLIST MANCEUVRES. "ABANDONING WARRINGTON."

It would appear that the volunteer cyclist has already become an established institution, although it is only about fifteen months ago since for the first time a corps of volunteer cyclists "marched" past the Commander-in-Chief at a review. Since then the cyclists have evinced great interest in the move- ment, and have had their own independent spring manoeuvres. Now the indefatigable Colonel Savile, who combines with his experience the energy of an enthusiast, is about to take advantage of Bank Holiday to conduct cyclist manoeuvres in Lancashire and Cheshire. As Warrington is one of the places to be visited, particulars of the proposed manoeuvres will be read with interest. The manoeuvres are to be carried out on August 4,5, and 6, under com- mand of Colonel Savile. The general idea on which they will be based is that an enemy has landed at Southport. The defender's troops in the immediate vicinity are covering Liver- pool and Manchester. The enemy's cavalry has been seen at Wigan on the afteahoon of Saturday, August 4, and it is consequently deemed advisable to re- move all stores from Warrington, and then abandon the place, destroying the bridges over the river Mersey. The general officer commanding the de- fenders at Crewe sends forward a cyclist flying column at ten D.M. on Saturday, August 4, to cover the removal of stores at Warrington, and then on abandoning the place, to destroy the bridges over the Mersey. The enemy appearing in force at Warrington, the place is abandoned at 11 a.m. on the sth, and the cyclist flying column is directed to retire by various routes to the Altrincham-Chester- road, and to watch that line with a cordon of cyclist patrols. The exact extent of front covered will de- pend upon the number of cyclists in the field. In- structions for the continuation' of the manoeuvres on Monday, August 6, will be issued according to the existing circumstances on Sunday evening, in time for the men to take trains, arriving at their respective destinations the same night. The cyclists will arrive at Warrington on Saturday, and will spend that evening and Sunday morning in practising all the evolutions of scouting, skir- mishing, and reporting that would properly belong , to so serious an operation as the abandonment of Warrington and the destruction of its valuable bridges. Regarding the arrangement the "Man- chester Guardian" observes :—" We are rather sorry to 'see that in the inevitable make-believe, without which manoeuvres cannot be carried on, there is so much running away. If an enemy were in reality to try to land at Southport, we hope and believe that the Manchester Brigade of Volunteers, with the Manchester Artillery, would be there in time to prevent his succeeding. But even if be landed and was so rash as to move towards Wigan, the Liverpool Volunteers would surely make themselves too disagree- able for him to advance far; while a company of Lord Crawford's excellent corps would give a good account of his cavalry scouts at Wigan. If the Laneashire people are to be represented as so panic- stricken as the scheme implies, it would have been kind to have imagined some formidable enemy ad- vancing after a great victory. But of course the suppositions are arranged so as to find an excuse to "evacuate Warrington," which is the particular operation that has been chosen for the cyclists to practise. Rumour says that these manoeuvres are to have specially interesting features not before seen in cyclist operations. At any rate the work will be well done, for there are in Lancashire Volun- teer Cyclists second to none."

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

The inaugural ceremony in connection with the Church House in London took place on Saturday. Judge Bishop at D010.311y. on Monday, non-suited the rector of the parish, who claimed 10s. burial fees from a Nonconformist for burying the latter's child.

- The Bryngvryn, an iron vessel of 1,226 tons, belonging to Liverpool, has been wrecked at Carimata Passage, and only part of the crew were saved. The proprietors of the Ocean Colliery Co., Rhondda Valley, have voluntarily decided to grant an advance of 5 per cent. to their 5,000 colliers. - -

It is off "- announced that the Queen will visit Paisley 01' 23. fler Majesty is to be presented with an a, • ,of welcome by the Town Council. In the Divorce Division, on Monday, a decree, with -nets, was granted to Mr. Piercy Radclife, on account of his wife's misconduct with the co-respondent, Mr. Pita. roy Somerset, with whom she had eloped. The parties lre well known in Liverpool sporting circles. A woman named Millward was sentenced to six months' imprisonment at Birmingham, on Monday, for cruelty to her daughter, a girl of 14. The latter had lien so severely beaten by her mother that she jumped from the bedroom window, and afterwards attempted to drown herself.

At Westminster Police Court, on Monday, Mrs. Gordon Bane, her husband, Robert Frost, and her butler, Robert Gigner, were again brought up for examination on various charges of obtaining money by means of worthless cheques. The prisoners were committed for trial, bail being refused.

A charge of seriously wounding his wife and daughter with a razor wrss preferred at the Liverpool Police Court, on Monday, again George Roberts, an elderly man who lives at Sleepers' fill. A doctor's certificate was suh• milted showing that the prisoner was temporarily in- sane. Art mand was minted.

A young man named Arthur Moss was committed for trial to the assizes at Nottingham, on Monday, charged with causing grievomOodily harm to Alford Hind, a well. Nottingham athlete. Hind has had his left arm permanently injured through a shot. After turning out of an hotel one night last October, it was alleged that Moss fired a gun, which he carried. liii a civil action £750 damages were awarded, but nothing was paid. The report of the committee appointed by the Tree- wry to inquire into the system of conducting the legal business of the e;overninent was published on Monday. The committee find that the Staff of the Solicitor to the Treasury Department is decidedly in excess of what is necessary, that many members of the staff are paid too highly, and that the working hours are too few. Various reforms are recommended by the committee. - •

SUDDEN DEATH OF A YORKSHIRE BAROVRT.—Sir John Swale, Bart.. of Knaresborough, was found dead in bed on Monday morning, having died from syncope. He was 51 years of age, and for some time had)Deen the pro- nrietor and landlord of the Royal Oak Hotel and Restau- rant. The deceased gentleman leaves four daughters, and the title will descend to one of the uncles, Mr. Ben- jamin Swale, of Knaresborough, who is 72 years of age. Early on Sunday morning a servant girl, while asleep, left the house where she was employed in Bath with only er night-dress on. She walked to another house where a girl she knew was employed, and knocked at the door, but received no answer. The somnambulist then walked two miles out of the city, eventually being stopped by two men, who Leek her to the hospital at Bath. After being in bed some hours she awoke, apparently none the worse for her adventure.

A woman named Robinson, and child 14 months old, were going to bed, the mother carrying the child and' lamp. The baby snatched at the lamp, knocked it out of the mother's hand, and set. her on fire. They were in the house alone, but the woman's shrieks caused neigh- bours to burst the door open, when the mother and child were found in flames. They were extinguished, and the sufferers taken to the Scuthern Hospital, Liverpool, where they both died on Sunday bight. At Shropshire Assizes on Monday, before Mr. Justice Denman, Elizabeth Evans, single woman, sought to re- cover damages for breach of promise from Owen Owens, foreman at the Liverpool Waterworks at Llawat. Both parties are turned 50 years of age. The defendant met plaintiff at Oswestry in 1833, and remained engaged to ler up to October. 1887. In the following month, how. over, he married another woman. The defend 40t laiteeti the promise, and the jury awarded the plaintiff £75 damages. EXTENSIVE ROBBERIES BY A DOMESTIC SERVANT.—At he Bolton Police Court, on Monday, a domestic servant, 'lamed Annie Rushton. of no settled residence, was com- tnitteed to prison for 42 days for felony. The prisoner was in the habit of going about the town and getting a night's lodgings, decamping in the morning with a wantity of clothing, concealed under her ordinary dress. There were charges against her in Bolton, but she is wanted at Blackpool, Manchester, and other places for ke offences. A YLVORD BORSE-STEALING AT ROCTIDALE.—On MOB- Om- afternoon, at Rochdale, Charles Kershaw, who, the Chief Constable stated, had lately come out of prison, was charged with stealing a horse, the property of Thomas Fielding, of Holroyd-street. The prosecutor is a boolcireeper at Platt Bros., at Oldham, and on Satur- day morning, at 5 20, 'net the prisoner near Rovton, leading his horse, which he had stolen out of a field at Moss Bridge. The accused was committed to the Sessions for trial.• _

. A Smeoveteen's Witt..—A disputed point under the will of the late Mr. Charles Maclver was decided on Mon- day in the House of Lords. The questi m was whether Mr. David Maclver was liable to pay to the executors £5OO interest yearly on a sum of £lO,OOO which he had received from his father during the lifetime of the latter. Mr. Justice Smith, in the court below. fonnd in favour of Mr. D. Mechem., hut the Court of Appeal reversed that finding. The House of Lords now restored the judgment of Mr. Justice Smith, and allowed the appel- lant his costs. THE HYDE JUNCTION BATTIVAY ACCIDENT. Frank Culling, one of the persons injured in the accident, a week ago, at Hyde Junction, and who was taken to the Manchester Royal Infirmary, died there on Saturday night. His was the most serious ease among the injured, and all the week there has been little hope entertained of his recovery. He was very severely wounded on the head, and four or five of his ribs were fractured. The immediate cause of death is certified to be concussion of the brain. The deceased's wife was also injured in the collision, but not seriously% THE SHOCKING PARAFFIN LAHP OUTHAGE AT BOLTON. —At the Bolton Infirmary, on Saturday. a married woman; named Ann Mc.Donough, died from injuries re- neived during a quarrel with a neighbour woman, called Davies. On a recent Saturday night the women had a quarrel, and during the altercation Davies seized a lighted paraffin lamn from the table, and hurled it at "Mc.Donough. The glass broke, and the oil becoming Ignited, the woman was soon enveloped in flames. She rushed into the street scream- ing wildly in her agony, and eventually a gentleman with the aid of his dust co % extinguished the flames, but not before the poor woman had been terribly burned about the head and body. She was removed to the Infirmary and Davies was arrested, and stands in- dicted, for the Liverpool Assizes, on the charge of in- flicting grievous bodily harm on Mc.Donough. At the inquest, on Monday, a verdict of "Wilful murder" was returned against Davies. Mn. GLADSTONE'S VOICE TO DE HEARD IN AMERICA. --A phonograph will arrive at Mr. Thomas A. Edison's laboratory, at Llewellyn Park, within a day or two, which, when it is allowed to give forth the sounds that are contained within it, will create no small degree of sensation. It contains the tones of the eloquent voice of William E. Gladstone, ex-Premier of England, the "Grand Old Man," who is now Ireland's dearest advo- cate. Still more, there is sealed up in the little instru- ment a song by the diva Adelina Patti. and a speech by the Right Hon. Arthur Jas. Balfour, Chief Secretary for Ireland. Mr. Edison sent this most perfect of all his phonographs to England some months ago with the idea of obtaining for the edification of the American people the sounds of the voices of the great English statesment, Gladstone and Balfour, as well as ?hose of the divine Patty, whose last and only farewell tour is Still fresh in the memory of all lovers of music in this country. The iniesion was a success, and the phonograph, full of eloquence and song, is almost hourly expected to arrive. When Mr. Edison shall finally turn the crank which shall unwind the skein of language and music, a treat may be expected such as may n,ver be experienced again until Gladstone. Balfour, and Itatti shall come in propria persona,. When asked last evening as to the time of the phonograph's arrival, Mr. Edison said, "It will be here by the next steamer."—New York July 10th. MR. GLADSTONE ON INDUSTRIAL 00-OPERATION.—The Co-operative News on Saturday published the follow- ing letter from Mr. Gladstone, in reply to an in- vitation to speak at a Co-operative Festival to he held at the Crystal Palace on Saturday, August 18 :—"Sir,—lt will not he in my power to attend the important meeting which you describe, but I have no difficulty in giving an opinion as to its object, based on such information as I possess; only ~eretting that it is notmore adequate and complete. I eertainly am under the belief that co-operative supply for the working classes has been the instrument of very great advantage, social and moral, as well as economical; that it has on the one hand husbanded their resources, and on the other confirmed the habit of thrift and the sense of self-reliance and independence. To an agency so powerful and so beneficial I tender my warm acknow- ledgements, with my alone that it may be even more Prosperous and efficient in the future than in the past. regard co-operative production as having special ases of its own, and as, on the whole, in its principle, not less beneficial than co-operation for supply, but as more difficult of execution, and as requiring the most cautious scrutiny of means and ends in each particular case. I give those opinions with diffi- dence, as resulting only from distant observation; and I make no reference here to the system of co-operative supply among classes in easier circumstances, which I regard less as a positive institution than as a remedial plan brought into existence by the thoroughly vicious character of the system of long credits and proportion- ately high prices that forms, to so large an extent, the basis of retail denlings in the metropolis, and perhaps elsewhere.—l remain, sir, your obedient and faithful servant (Signed) W. E. GLADSTONE.—A. L. Hannay, Esq."

The Marquis of Hart locum, M.P. for Rossenciabkhad leader of the Liberal Unionist party, completed hie 561kh year on Monday. It is understood Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone will Lemma London the second week in August, to spend the recess at Hawarden.

The Press Association save it is now considered prac- tically settled that there Will he an autumn session. the House rising for summer holidays in the second week in August The Marquis of Salisbury has sent to the Ballywena Orangemen an acknowledgment of a resolution appal.- lag of the Government policy. The Premier says that this expression on the part of a great number of persons, and the immense weight which such an expression must carry with it, have impressed him greatly, and he values vtry highly this testimony of approval. Mn. GLADSTONK AND SUNDAY CLOTNO.—TIir! Rev. DlM- son Burns, of the United Kingdom Alliance, having written to Mr. Gladstone with reference to his speech at. Sir Wilfrid Lawson's, that he appeared to refer to the hill of Lord It. Grosvenor as having the same object as Mr. Stevenson's for the closing of public-houses on Sun• days, has received the following reply, dated the 21st inst.:—" I am directed by Mr. Gladstone to thank you for your letter, and to say that he had no idea of conveying the impression that the two bills referred to were iden- tical in object." Mr. Jacob Bright. M.P., addressing a gathering of Liberals of South-West Manchester on Saturday, at Rnutsford, after a picnic to Tables', referred to the deaths of Mr. John Mandeville and Dr. Ridley, and said that he thought these circumstances would arouse a feeling throughout the kingdom which woWd be disastrous to the Government and to the policy which the Government was pursuing in Ireland. With regard to the proposed Commission of Judges, he said he regarded it as charac- teristically unfair. It appeared as if the Government, since they pallid not make the Irish leaders bankrupt In character, were endeavouring to make them bankrupt its means.

BUTED TO EGAN "VILE FORGERIES."

The Irreernan's Journal publishes the folkoVing cable- gram from Mr. Patrick Egan, received last night:-.- " Lincoln.—Freeman telegram received. Every one of letters attributed to me hy Attorney-General Tile forgeries. One of the most imnortant, 24th February, 1881, dated from 99, Avenue de Villiers, Paris. I never resided at that address until DAcember, 1881. From 4th February to July, that year, lived at Hotel Brighton. Rue le Rivoli. This can be verified from hotel books.—PATII. ROAN." _ _

The Freeman's Journal London correspondent says that confirmatory of the statement of Mr. Egan, that he did not reside in the Avenue De Villiers for several months after the date of the letter bearing that address, which the Attorney-General attributed to him in the roDonnell trial, Mr. Egan was getting the Nation news- paper in Paris, and on receipt of his cablegram, on satnrday, Mr. J. D. Sullivan verified this by referring to the Nation's subscribers' book. In these he found the dates in Mr. Egan's cablegram absolutely confirmed, that ,he Nation was sent to the Dote! Brighton until July Bth, when Mr. F-n changed his address. The letter alleged to have h.-, ••i`t..n by Mr. Egan from the Avenue De Villiers is ii February fitti, when he was living at the hotel already mentioned, inn different part of Paris.

ANNUAL MEETTNG OF THE COBDEN CLUB. The annual general meetin,, was held on Saturday at the National Liberal Club. Mr. T. It-Pcrmstz, M.P., who presided, said he sew no reason whatever to despair of the ultimate -acceptance of the principles of the Cobden Club. On the Continent I here was a war of tariffs raging between Various Pro- tectionist countries, which would cause such bacon- *vonience that ere long the advantages of a system of *roe exchange would he recognised. In America the burden of Protection has been so great that the taxpayers seemed earnest in their efforts for relief and doubtless their example would have a great effect all over the world. At home the threatened attack last :mtumn on our fiscal system had not succeeded as its iTomoters desired. With reference to the protection of the tended interest, lie said he believed that garden cut- tire in favoured spots, considering the unlirnited demand tor its products, would be greatly to the advantage of the 'landowner, and could be wisely encouraged by smaller tioldings, and facilities for purchase, and he did. not de- pair of seeing a groat effort made at storage of ,rater and irrigation for agricultural and horticultural purposes. The Cobden Club, being impressed with the A-eat importance of this question, are about to publish series of works on the development of the resources of he soil. If the landowners will take the subject into their earnest cosideration, and make the most of the i‘roduction of the soil, and also clear away the obstacles •A-bich now mist between them as producers and the ::reat body of the consumers, in whatever shape they resent themselves, they may find that their interests ;quire no protection, and they may cease to hanker after restoration of food taxes. The report was adopted, and it WAS decided to post- riP the dinner until next year,

div.head: THUNDERSTORM.
div.p: THE THUNDERSTORM.
Various parts of Torkshiro, Lancashire, Cheshire, and the Midlands were visited by a thunderstorm on Monday.

A miner, working on the pit bank at Brynn, near Wigan, was killed on Monday by lightning. A second man was disabled. At Stockton, Considerable damage was done to grass crops by a heavy rainfall. On Monday at noon the schoolroom at Walton. belong- ing to Miss Pilkington, sister of Sir L. M. S. Pilkington, of Chevet Park, and of which Mr. G. Bott is the master, was struck by lightning, and the building was much damaged, and also the desks and benches. There were only a few children who had brought their dinners in the schoolroom at the time, all of whom escaped with- out injury. A heavy thunderstorm broke over Birmingham be- ,ween one and two o'clock on Monday. in the course of which the lightning struck Messrs. Coves gun manu- factory, in Woadcock-atreet. A saw mill in the yard and a cottage adjoining were badly damaged, but no personal injuries were sustAined. The storm was of ex- ceptional severity, the downfall of rain being enormous At Skipton, at noon. the el^ctric fluid struck the house of Mr. John Hogg, in Keighlel -road, knocking down the chimney, which fell loon a small conservatory at the hack, the roof of the Atter being entirely demolished. A number of slates were broken, and one end of the house was smashed in, causing considerable damage. The family were away at Blackpool. and the servant WAS the only occupant of the premises. She was not injured. The electric fluid eso struck the ,house of Mr. John Gill, at the extreme end of the same block of buildings, breaking the chimney, and taking away portions of the roof. Lightning shocks also took place at other houses in Newtown and Middletown. but no damage is reported. Another severe storm occurvil between four and five o'clock in the afternoon, the heavy rainfall nearly causing a flood.

411 Gas Question in Warrington still occupies liC attention, and will continue to do so until Present crisis is past. It is now regarded as lx3Y'rid doubt that the majority of the seem- of the Gas Committee will formally On at the forthcoming meeting of the Town 17arici1. We do not for 'ourselves see that they oa're good grounds for taking so extreme a course. tilt's item only of their programme was sent back— with regard to the appointment of a consult- and even as to this the Council was e°llsiderate as to sanction the appointment for kve months. Why, then, should the Committee ? Do they wish to lay down the hard and line that it must be taken as an expression of of confidence, if the Council should think fit ,tsieet or alter any proposal of any Committee? scarcely think the Gas Committee will commit Ayes to such a doctrine ; for that were to say each Committee is looked upon as infallible, 'therefore beyond the supervision of the Conn- as a Whole. It is, we grant, a different thing if are prepared to urge that they regard the ap- at of a consulting engineer as of such im- tee that they decline to accept the responsi- of managing the Gas Works if their proposal ‘l,4lll°t accepted. But we do not expect that they aay anything of the kind; for we anticipate that the resignations will not be accepted, and that °onituittee will proceed with their work as liapef ore, after being assured that the Council 411c't lost confidence in them. 4uming that the difficulty is got over, what we 1114 recommend is that the Committee should tCtlkt their attention to the various suggestions irlei,have been offered for their consideration both kttt7 and outside the Town Council. 1' alce the v,ita7r of the price of gas, which is the Chief thing the till° hulk of the gas consumers. We hold that the,,..tute has come for the Committee to put kit4elvesin a position to announce a reduction, e,,,L'ugh the reduction may be small. Other 10°rations, and private companies, have recently 1,(Z: reductions, and we do not see why a similar 4111. should not be bestowed upon -Warrington. It will be seen that the aver- age of "gas unaccounted for" is 6.5, thus cor- responding with the average of 6.26 for Runcorn, 'Widnes, and St. Helens. As the leakage this year for Warrington is close on 16 per cent., it would seem that the "unsatisfactory leakage" is not 4 per cent., as inferred by the chairman of the Gas Committee, but more than double that—it is from 9to 10 per cent. A large leakage may be said tO be inevitable in mining districts, where gas mains are injured by subsidences; but Warrington is not a mining town; and we take it that no reasonable person will deny that there is need for .a thorough investigation when its leakage is found to be more than double the average of the rest of the country.

ISOTH CARLYLE and RUSKIN have written pointedly and vigorously on the necessity of find- ing a solution of the difficult problem which is raised by the antagonistic relations between labour and capital, It is a common thing to say that their interests are identical, and so they are in so far as they both journey together with the object of obtaining full reward for their services. It is 'when it comes to be determined what shall be the reward in each case that antagonism sets in; the quarrel is, so to speak, as to the division of the spoil. Hitherto capital, as the stronger of the two, has taken the lion's share, and labour has been not a little dissatisfied. The difficulty is to make an arrangement which will be satisfactory to all parties to the transaction; and the latest suggest- tion is that this can best be accomplished by moats of partnerships of industry. One of tlieSo is al- ready at work, and its operations art being watched from many quarters with the keenest in- terest. It is being conducted at the Wood- house Mills, Huddersfield, the business hav- ing been converted into a Limited Company upon the basis of taking the workpeople into part- nership. 93rlefly," the management say, "our principles are, first a payment of five per cent. up- on capital, whether loan or shares; after providing for this, and a formation of a reserve fund of not less than ten per cent. of the profits until it amounts, to ten per cent. of the capital, the re- maining profits will be divided as follows :—five- ninths will go to the credit of each worker, who has been employed six months, in proportion' to the wages earned; and with a view to encouraging honest manufacture and honest trading, the re- maining four-ninths may be applied in making al- lowances to custom, thus binding more closely to- , gether all parties most concerned in a business that leads to regular employment." The committee are all working-men; but the manager is Mr. GEORGB THOMPSON, who was at the head of the firm when it was a private undertaking. He has thrown himself heart and soul into the movement, and has put the woollen mill as a going concern into the hands of the new company upon tereas which preclude the possibility of anything being

paid as promotion money. Mr. RUSKIN, writing some time ago of the project, said :—"I cannot enoug. h thank you, or express the depth of my pleasure, in the announcement of the momentous and absolutely foundational step taken by you, in ali that is wise and just, in the establishment of these relations with your workmen." The leaqrs of he co-operative movement are of course anxious that the projectshould succeed; but it would seem that private traders regard what is being don, with a jealous eye, for we learn that some of the wholesale customers do not like the idea of dealing with a firm which includes the workpeople as part- ners. This is a selfish and narrow view to take of the enterprise and we trust the Company, by bringing their goodg before the public and making, as they do, a really good article, will secure a large portion of the pub 4 favour. From the first balance sheet which has been issued it would ap- pear that, after allowing ten per cent, for deprecia- tion, interest at the rate of five per cent. has been paid on loan stock, and a dividend of five per cent. has been paid upon shares. Beyond this, there was a balance of nearly £lOO wltich the members have applied in writing off formation expenses. This may be regarded as a good start; and it is not too much to hope that there will be something in addition, next year, to" go to the credit of each worker, who his been employed six months, in proportion to the wages earned." It is not for mortals to command success; but they may, as in this case, do more—they may deserve it.

Lin night there was a meeting of the Town Council to receive and consider a statement which had been prepared by the Sanitary Committee with regard to Longford Depot. The statement, which we give in another column,. shows a balance on the wrong side of 2981 7s 7d, and Alderman BUR- GESS, as Chairman of the Committee, frankly admitted that they were not getting the results that had been• anticipated. He said the ,Com- mittee were making the best of the difficulty, an that the management of the works was not what it &Mild be. Councillor Morms had, however, previously travel:4o the whole subject of the expenditure and income of the present sanitary system; and it will be seen that he pill Ossa upon Pelion, in the way of figures, to demon- strate that there was a wide margin between original promise and actual performance. So far, he said, was the present system from proving the success that was expected, that, instead of reducing the cost of dealing with the town's refuse, it was largely increased. Notwith- standing an expenditure of over £20,000, his con- tention was that the annual cost per closet had increased frOul 40. 50, ill 1.5* 49 $4. 114 d, in 1888. lb &pia, =No thin the ratepayeki with him in urging, that the whole question of machinery and management would require sifting from top to bottorn before the Council could be called upon to incur further expenditure. Alder- man BURGESS complimented Councillor MoNss on his able statement, and admitted the force of much that he had to say, but held that the issue was less a question of cost than of the health, comfort, ,an convenience of the public. Unfortunately he was not permitted to fini& his speech ; attention was called to the fact that, whilst he was speak- ing, there had ceased to be a quorum, and the pro- ceedings were brought to a "most lame and impo- tent conclusion." Perhaps we ought to say "im- pudenti conclusion,". for we have reason to know that some of the members of the Council—and even of the Sanitary Committee—left the Council Chamber in order to bring toa farcical termination what should have ,been an important discussion. This may be sport—of a kind; but it is not busi- ness. It was little less than an insult to Alderman BURGESS as an individual, and it was a discredit to the Town Council as a body.

"TOUCH AND GO."

- - - - Wednesday last was the golden wedding celebra- tion of Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone. Blessings on them ! In view alike of their greatness and their goodness, may we not say, with Milton: Hither, as to their fountain, other stars Repairing, in their golden urns, draw light ?

St. Helens volunteers are marksmen; their hits are always palpable at Wimbledon. This year they have taken in the way of prizes £l6O 10s 6d, one gold jewel, one bronze jewel, two bronze crosses, and nine badges. Again we have to say —" Well done, St. Helens 1" General Boulanger is a very much beaten man ; he was beaten in the Chamber as a speaker; he was beaten on the sod as a duellist; and now •he is beaten in the Ardoche as a candidate. Boulan- ' orim is a farce which is pretty nearly played out.

A novel by a Warrington lady is novel; and has given birth to a conundrum. People are asking— In what way did Mrs. Mc fall? And the answer is—by writing " Ideala." [N.B.—This, as "A. Ward" would say, is a " goilk " ; Mrs. McFall really rises in the estimation of those wl4o have read her clever work.]

-- The Moloch of paraffin week by week devours fresh victims. Two inquests were held in Liver- pool on Tuesday; in one case a woman, seventy years of age, had been burned to death; and in the other a mother and her child perished through fire from a paraffin lamp., The Legislature insists on a safety lamp for the mine. Is it not time to enforce a safety lamp for the household F

The Pope knows "what's what" too well to think of putting Ireland under bell and book. His latest reported utterance is as mild as mother's milk. "His last rescript concerning Ireland must be considered as a proof of his interest in that un- happy country. The Pope added that a solution of the Irish question which would satisfy all parties would give him much pleasure." And so say all of us.

Sir Wilfrid Lawson, referring to the arrest of Mr. O'Kelly, M.P. asked, in the House of Com- mons on Wednesday, if it was true that since the House broke up the previous night a member had been arrested. But he couldtet no information. The Attorney-General said Sir Wilfrid should be "more specific "—as if M.P.'s were being arrested every night. To this complexion have we come at last, Horatio.

Mr. O'Kelly was arrested in London on Tuesday evening, and the charge against him is that of "inciting to boycotting in Ireland." Inciting Neither an English nor an Irish Liberal can make a speech in Ireland without bringinghimself within the reach of the Crimes Act. But the Govern- ment do not dare to arrest an English member of Parliament for inciting to boycotting. The Crimes Act is a brutal and cowardly thing—as brutal and cowardly as its authors.

-- At Liverpool, on Wednesday, a butcher named I Arthur Fisher was fined 50s. and costs for "ex- posing for sale meat unfit for human food." Mr. Marks, who prosecuted, said as to the meat—" Not only was it horseflesh, but it was old horseflesh, diseased horseflesh and decomposed horseflesh, and it was exposed for sale without being labelled as horseflesh." A fine of 50s. is too little for selling such horseflesh; the toucii of a horsewhip, and a fine of £5 would have been more to the purpose.

Let river pollutors beware; the Salford Corpora- tion has struck a blow and drawn blood. The Hey- wood Corporation, at the instance of the authori- ties of Salford, have been ordered by a County Court Judge to " USW their funning" in the way

of fouling a tributary of,the Irwell with abomin- able sewage. Thve are other offenders—over a score of them—to be dealt with before anything like pure water can be expected in the channel of the Mersey, and (finally) the bed of the Ship Canal. It is to be hoped that they will all be County Courted, Ind that right speedily.

Mr.McLaren; M.P., has done the right thing in warning Mr. Long, M.P., that he will call atten- tion to his conduct as a member of the Govern- ment in going to 'Rochester to, speak in support of Colonel Hughes-Hallett. If Hallett were a weaver or a collier and had done what he has done' his former comrades would show their regard for decency by boycotting him. The Government do not boycott him; they send two of their officials to back him up I The offence smells rank in the nostrils of men like Mr. McLaren. The line odght to be drawn somewhere; let it be drawn at the Hughes-Halletts.

_ After trying to white-wash inch a I;rlackamoor as the member for Rochester, the Government are doing everything they can to besmurch the Chaf- acters of thn Parnellites, without furnishing a particle of evidence in supiiart of their foul charges. They have gloated over the, opportunity which the "Times" has given them of insinuating that Air. Parnell has been guilty of furnishing money to the vilest scoundrels for the purposes of. assassmatcon. But when asked to appoint a Select Committee of inquiry they shrink back; Clay shirk the issue. , .

Mr. Parnell gave Mr. Smith a trouncing on Monday night—Mr. Smith, who wanted to intro- duce an important bill without debate, and has had to back out of a false and stupid position. It is signifitant that, whereas, in the first instance, Mr. Smith spoke of a Commission to inquire into the charges against members of Parliament, he has brought in a bill to 'include "other persons." He had an idea that he might draw out that leviathan Parnell with a hook; now he is content to whip the smallest stream for the little fishes.

If the members of the Government really believe Mr. Parnell ,has written the letters which the "Times" attributes to him, it is their duty to bring him before a jury under an indictment of conspiracy to murder. He ought to have no choiee in the matter;. and, if the case were proved, he ought to "swing at the end of's string." But, as Mr. Parnell told them, they haven't the cour- age of their grandmother. They dare not take the hull by the horns, and confiiie themselves to the real issue; they will do anything but that.

There is either a great tura:* of indifference or a great deal of bungling among the magis- trates of the •Prescot district. It is simply disgraceful that people Should be kept waiting for an hour and a half, as was the case on Tues- day, until magistrates can be hunted up. And, after all, some of the eases had to be adjourned because two magistrates could not be kept to- gether until thn business was ',finished. This is a mockery of justice. The victims should complain to the Home Secretary; or ask some member 9f xilriiprilt to bring the matter before th 4

,A. London contemporary is disposed .to poke fun at the St. Helens Town Council for hesitating to increase the salary of the librarian from .£l2O £10; but criticism, like charity ~ourilit to begin at home. There are very few districts in the metropolis that can bring themselves to applying the Libraries Act at all, and they do not, there- fore, spend a penny on a librarian. And then how many thousands of houses there are in London that are not supplied with gas The "men of light and leading" in St. Helens are, according to their means, a long way ahead of their critics in the big city.

Pamphlet "How to preserve the sight" free on application. —Ada THE WIDNES DIVORCE Can.—Mr. R. White Side, ac- countant and auctioneer, Victoria-road, Widnes, has been appointed receiver in the divorce suit, Garton v. Garton, by Sir James Hannan, of the High Court. HOLY TRINITY DAY SCHOOITS, RUNCORN. The results of the Government Examination in connection with this school have been made known. The infants have earned the ekcellent grant; in the girls' department the passes average 93 per cent., and the results of the boys' depart- meat are equallY good., Sr. JOHN'S rinforrsaran SUNDAY SCHbOL RUNCORN. —The scholars and friends of the Sunday School connec- tedwith St. John's Presbyterian Chapel, Runcorn, spent an enjoyable day at Overton Hills on Monday. To the number of 100 they started from Runcorn in six convey- ances supplied by Mr. James Peck, about one o'clock, and arrived at Overton shortly after two, Owing to the excellent accommodation provided the pleasures of the 'party were little interfered with by the occasional showers of rain. A capital tea was provided and full justice was done to it. FIRE id nuNwoaru.—Abeut ten 'o'clock on Sunday night the barn belonging to Mr. Hulme, of Peel House- lane, Farnworth, was chscotered to be on fire, and in response to the alarm that was raised, the Widnes Fire Brigade was•quickly on the spot. A number of ' police constables also put in an appearance, but notwithstand- ing the united efforts of brigade and police under the direction of Mr. I. Carr and Inspector Keighley, the barn was completely destroyed, along with its contents— newly mown hay from 11 acres of lansl—and entails con- siderable loss upon the owner. There is no clue as to how the fire originated. METHODIST FREE Cuu`ncif, RUNCORN. -- The anniver- sary of the Sunday school in connection with the United Methodist Free Church, Ellesmere-St., Runcorn, was celebrated on Sunday. Both morning and evening the sacred edifice was crowded, especially in the evening, and the services were conducted by the Rev. J. B. Stone- man, of Liverpool. A novel feature in the rev, gentle- man's preaching was an interval in the sermon during which he sang a sacred solo. As Xi.. Stoneman is the possessor of a pleasing tenor voice his singing was much enjoyed. Under the leadership of Mr. John Holford, the choir and scholars rendered anthems and hymns specially selected for the occasion. In the afternoon a flower service of song" was rendered by the choir and scholars, the connective readings being given by Mr. John D. Jones, of High-St. The chapel was charmingly decora- ted with cut flowers and plants, and presented a very pretty appearance. Collections in aid of the school funds were taken at each service, and amounted to £24 2s 6d. Sold in bottles, Id., 2d., and 3d.—lstutc Stubbs, Lowlands-road, Run ooen.—Adve.

I A SUCCESSFUL RUNCORNIAN.—WiIIiam Henry Wood, son of the Rev. George Wood, and apprentice to Mr. Wilton, druggist, Higli-st., passed the preliminary ex- amination of the Pharmaceutical Society of Greatßritain oil the 10th inst., and is now duly registered as an ap- prentice or student. SUCCESSFUL Loom, Bewr.Eas.—A main of bowls was played at the Garston Hotel on Thursday afternoon, in which a number of local bowlers competed, and were very successful. The first and second pries, amounting togetker to £2 10s, were divided between Mr. H. Baines, of Garston, and Mr. W. Wright, of Runcorn, whilst the third (10s) was secured by Mr. W. J. Moreland. The fourth and fifth prizes (7s 6d each) were respectively won by Mr. R. Wright, of Runcorn, and Mr. Sutton, of Garston. WIDNES COUNTY COURT.—At this court yesterday, be fore his Honour Judge Thompson, N. Traghien, of Man- chester, sued Francis Cooke, grocer, of Alforde-et., for the sum of £1 19s 11d, value of a chest of tea supplied. Mr. F. J. Poole appeared for the defendant, the plaintiff was unrepresented. The defence was that the plaintiff had merely left the tea with the defendant until he could find a customer for it.. His Honour suggested that it I would be best to settle the case, and Mr. Poole arranged that the tea should be returned on the understanding ' that the case was withdrawn. The case was accordingly withdrawn. At Runcorn Police Court on Tuesday, a man named William Knight, was charged with having stolen a vest and a blue silk handkerchief, the property of John Hornsley, a Ship Canal navvy.--lfornsley lived at a house in Poole-lane, and the prisoner also took up his abode in the same house. On the 18th June the prisoner took his departure, and the articles were subsequently missed. A man named Joseph Henry Houghton saw him wearing the 'Waistcoat, but he disappeared and was not traced until he was apprehended in Chester.—The prisoner,who alleged that he had been apprehended in mistake for his brother, was romanded until Monday next. ' A Viola:NT RUNCORN WOMAN.—Before Mr. Brundrit and Mr. Thomas, at Runcorn Police Court on Tuesday, Ellen Barker, a single, woman, of Pool-lane, was charged with having, o i the 17th inst., assaulted Walter Bee, a man who lotbses in the same neighbourhood. During the altercation between the parties the woman struck the man on the face with a quart jug she carried in her hand. The jug was smashed, and the man's nose suffered severely from the blow. A fineof lOs and costs, 8s 6d, was imposed.—The prisoner was further charged with having been drunk in the court-house on the pre- vious day, and she was fined 5s and costs, or seven days' hard labour, for this offence.—The woman went to gaol for 21 days. SWINE FEvER IN RUNCORN DIVISION.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions. on Monday, Thomas Clough, butcher, Church-st., wa.s,charged with having on the lith July, caused certain swine to be moved into an infected area without having a license.—Alfred Daniels was charged with having moved the pigs.—J.S. Jones said he met Daniels in Halton. He was driving a spring cart con- taining three pigs, and said that Mr. Clough had pur- chased them at the Ermine Hotel, thester, and had sent him for them. The defendant Clough said the Inspector told him that Chester was " clear ' from swine fever, and he could move the pigs anywhere. Superintendent Hollingworth said Runcorn Police Division was declared an infected area. The defendants were each fined Is and costs, 8s 6d. • MUSICAL HONOeRS FOR WIDNES.—We are pleased to re- cord the highly successful manner in which Miss Beatrice Parkes, daughter of Mr. H. Parkes, of Frederick-st.„ Widnes, has passed the recent examinations held in Liver- pool in connection with• the Trinity College of Music, London, in pianoforte playing. She has taken senior honour certificate with a further recommendation by the examiner to sit for the higher examination in the colles,,e, London. She also passe an examination in December last for musical knowledge, obtaining a eestifleate in the junior division, taking the full number of one hundred marks. She is only foarteen years of age, and has al- ready obtained four certificates from Trinity College, London. She is the pupil of my*, and the Misses Barfoot, St. lichens. • IsrociatNT TnErr AT RAINCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, a navvy named Thomas Jones was charged with stealing a blue handkerchief and a bodice, the property of William Craddock, pawnbroker, 'Church- st. On Saturday night the prisoner entered Mr. Crad- dock's shop, and after examining various articles, left without having made a purchase.. Afterwards the hand- kerchief was missed from a hook at the doer. Mr. Craddock jun. saw the prisoner fumble amongst some clothing at the door, and then put the bodice under his , arm, and exclaim to a person in the street, "I will go in and pledge it." He wslked into the shop and offered the bodice in pledge, and was at once given into custody. He was wearing the blueliantikerchief round his neck at the time. The prisoner was remanded for a week so that inquiries might be made into his antecedents. MARRIED MISERY AT RUNCORN.—George Dunbabin, a furnaceman, was summoned before the Runcorn magis- trates on Monday, to answer a charge of deserting his wife Sarah Ann.—The complainant said amp had been married 8 years, and had lived together until the 26th June. He then Mused her and deserted her, and she had since lived with her mother. There was only one child, and her mother kept that. The defendant, when they lived together, sometimes gave her 14s and 15s per week, and sometimes nothing. He was in the habit of drinking.—The defendant said he was not likely to give his wife money when sho would go • out and come back drunk without having purchased any provisions. He ac- cused his wife of committing adultery, but failed to bring any witnesses.. The Bench ordered him to pay 53 per week towards his wife's maintenance. • • VIOLENT ASSAULT ON POLICEMEN AT WlDNES.—Williarn Burns, a young. man who lives in Catherine-st., was brought up charged with being drunk and disorderly, and also with assaulting Constables Almond and Davie. P.C. Almond stated that on Saturday afternoon he and P.C. Davie had a man in custody in Charlotte-st., when the prisoner, who was drunk, came behind them. He seized Almond by the throat, and/Struck him on the face with his fist; and in the struggle that ensued, Almond got the prisoner upon the ground. While putting the snaps upon him he kicked him several times on the ribs, and afterwards, whedstanding up. he kicked the con- stable on the knee, and disabled him for some time. The prisoner was then handed over to P.C. Davie, who was also severely kicked about the legs. The aid of two civilians had to be obtained to take the prisoner to the, pcilice station. The prisoner, who is an old offender, was sentenced to four months' hard labour. • STRANGE DROWNING AFFAIR AT WIDNES.—The deputy coroner, Mr. W. T. Husband, en Wednesday,' held an inquiry at the Commercial Inn. Widnes, into the circum- stances of the death of William Treacy, 42 years of age, who had lived at 10, Old Marsh. 'lt appeared that on Monday evening, about five o'clock, Treads- and his wife were walking home from Moss Bank by way of Mr. Ml- kington's works. Mrs. Trea.cy walked a little in advance of her husband, and, having crossed the railway, walked across thebridge to the other side of the canal. After walking about 150 yards she noticed her husband stand- ing on. the other side of the water, divested of his cloth- ing, with the exception of his singlet and drawers. Ho jumped into the water, apparently with the intention of swimming towards her, but he sank, and did not again rise to the surface.—The man was out of work, and it was thought that this had affected his mind slig,htly.— A verdict of "Accidental death" was recorded.—The Coroner commented upon the foolishness of attempting to swim in Water so filthy and poisonous. STADRE.D WITH A FORK AT WIDNES.—Refore Mr. Cl. Pilkington, at Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, Martha Woodside, a married woman, was charged with mali- ciously wcunding Sarah Alice Ellison wife of James Elli- son, of 24, West Bank-st. It was alleged that on Satur- day night Mrs Ellison was passing the door of prisoner's house in West Bank-st., when the prisoner called her a foul name, and then seizing hold of her by the hair dragged her into the lobby of her house. She suerPeded in releasing herself from the prisoner's grasp, but she at- tacked her again and stabbed her on the nose, head, and shoulder with a table fork. Mrs Ellison screamed "mur- der," and &labourer named Edward Rogers came upon the scene. At that time the fork was sticking in Mrs Ellison's head, and he took it out and threw it away. Mrs Ellison was bleeding very much, and he took her home. —Dr. Hutchinson described the wounds, and said they had evidently been made by a three proitged fork. It was fortunate that the blows had all been struck on bony parts Of the body, or the consequences would have been serious.—P.C. Halbrook stated that he apprehended the prisoner, who said "I only stabbed her once; she was rolling, on the floor and she got that on her nose whilst pressing on me. I did it in self defence."—The prisoner was committed to the assizes for trial. WOUNDED WITII A BRICK. AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. G. Pilkington. Timothy Candy, a youth. 16 years of age, was charged with having on the 21st inst., maliciously and feloniously wounded Mary Mullarkey, With intent to do her grievous bodily, harm. The prisoner was defended by Mr. F. J. Poole, The pirosecutrix stated that she was the wife of Thomas Mullarkely, and lived with him at 31, Moss Bank- road, Widnes. On Saturday afternoon the prisoner's mother, entered her house, and as she refused to leave, witness put her out. • Shortly afterwards the prisoner leaned over the back-yard wall and asked why she had " shoved " his mother out. Witness replied Wasn't it better for me to shovq your mother out than for my hus- band to come and kick her out." The prisoner said "I will murder you," and at the same time threw a brick at her. The missile struck her on the head, and she stag- gered against the wall. She bled very much from a wound on the head, and had not been out of the house until that morning. She 'was still very weak and ill. Elizabeth McGee, of 8, Little Mary-st., gave corrobora- tive evidence. Dr. O'Keeffe deposed that the woman was brought to his surgery at half-past six. She was suffering from a contused lacerated wound on the left side of the top of the head. The wound was two inches long, and penetrated to the bone. The woman's hair and clothes were covered with blood, and she was very faint A heavy brick like the one produced would cause the woune. P.C. Ratcliffe said he apprehended the prisoner at his parents house, 33, Moss Bank-road, on Sunday. He said "The woman threw a brick at me first, which missed me and struck the back door, and I picked up a little stone and threw it at her." The prisoner denied that he threw the brick produced and the constable said he had ascertained that it weighed five pounds. The prisoner was committed to the Assizes for trial. •

A BODY FOUND IN TEE RIVER AT. SUTTON.—OD Tues- day afternoon, the body of a man was found in the river Weaver, at Sutton. The man appeared to be about 40 years of age, and of the labouring class. Judging from the decomposed state of the body, it is conjectured that it has been in the water for two or three weeks. There were several bruises on the body, which appeared to have been caused after death, by either passing steamers or flats. The remains were removed to the Aston Arms, Sutton, and the coroner was communicated with. On Thursday an inquest was held on the, body at the Aston Arms, Frodsham Bridge, by Mr. J. E. Wonsley, coroner. Deceased was a stout-built nian, about 40 years of age, sft fin in height, brown hair, sandy moustache and im- perial, full face, and was attired in a black worsted coat and vest, moleskin trousers, nearly new, elastic-side shoes with iron tips, cotton stxiped shirt, blue flannel, and brown knitted socks.—The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned." ASSAULTING A RZNT BAILIFF AT WIDNES —On Thurs- day, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Matthew Broady, of 43, James-st., was summoned to answer a charge of assault- ing Lewis Colin, commission agent and rent bailiff.— Mr. J. W. Knowles represented the complainant.—lt was alleged that on Friday evening, the 20th inst.,Colien and an assistant entered the defendant's house to execute a distress warrant for arrears of rent amounting to £4. The defendant declared that they would remove nothing from that house, and pulling from his pocket a clasp knife, he threatened to" stick it into them "if they did not take their departure. Apprehending danger to their lives the men went out without much force being used, ind Con4tables Maitland and Cummings were brought .on thd scene. An entrance was again effected by open- ing the door, and then the defendant acted like a mad- man, and knocked the complainant and his assistant about like balls. lle struck Cohen several times on various parts of the body.—The defendant explained that he had the knife in his band because he was making a bow and arrow for his little boy, and denied that he had ever attempted to use it. Some person had acted in a scandalous fashion by telling Edward Wood, the renb collector, that he was about to sell his furniture, and thus induced him ,to put the bailiffs in. He had used no violence whateVer to the num.—The defendant, who, it was stated, had been a member in the Manchester City Police force, was fined ss, and costs 9s 6d.

• --- A WIDNES BOY'S FALL.—Walter Herbert, son of Mr. Herbert, Cholmondelev-street, Widnes, le as going down the steps at St. Relens station on Tues- day evening, when he fell with such violence on his face that the teeth completely perforated the lower lip, and he also received an ugly wound on the chin as well as a severe shOckp the whole system. The mother managed to get him home as quickly as pos- sible, wtere he now lies in a critical condition. Dr. Hutchinson has been constantly in attendance since the accident. A Winxes PIGEON FANCIER'S FALL,—A young man named Martin Cannon, of 18, West-st., was get- ting on a neighbour's wall a few days ago, trying to reach some pigeons, when the wall fell upon the top of him, including a large stone which weighed about four cwt. His legs were crushed in a shock- ing manner, but, strange to say, no bones were broken. He also received some injuries to his back, and had to be carried to his home, where he lies in great agony. being too, ill to be removed to the hos- pital. Dr. Hutchinson attended him, and he is pro- gressing asefireourably as can be expected. Tine ALLEGED PRIZE FlGHT.—Thomas McCor- mick. alias "Sparrow," of Union-st., St. Helens, and Joseph Anders, alias "Judy," of Crab-st., St. Helens, who were recently bound over at Newton Petty Sessions for a prize fight at Newton Common, were again brought up at the St. Helens Town Hall on Monday, before Aldermen J. Harrison and J. Mc- Bryde, for committing a breach of the peace, by fighting together, at Sutton, on the 14th inst. The defendants pleaded gufity.—Chief Constable Wood stated that the two men were engaged in a prize fight at Sutton. They were stripped, without shirts, and a large crowd of people had assembled. The people were "acking up" the defendants. The defendants fought once before, and were held to bail and now that they had pleaded guilty he (Chief Constable Wood) asked that they be bound over in sufficient sureties as would prevent any- thing of the kind again.—Wilfrid Johnson, 13 years I of age, stated that he knew the defendants, and on Saturday. the 14th hest., he saw them fighting with- out their shirts in a field at Sutton. He heard the .people "backing" them, and saying who would win.—The defendant Anders said they were not , fighting for money. Both of them were drunk, and • they did not fight fbr a penny.—The Bench bound 'each defendant over to keep the peace for three r months, themselves in .£lO, and two sureties of .C 5 each; in default of finding sureties, 14 days' im- prisonment. THE DISTRICT 00011 TEMPLAR CONVENTION.---1 The second meeting of the recently-formed South- West Lancashire Good Templar Convention was held at Golborne, in the Welsh Mission Room, on Saturday. All the lodges in the area were repre- sented, and there was a good attendance. Brother Morris Jones, D.S.. of Liverpool, presided. The Con- vention considered a suggested code of rules and by-laws submitted by a committee appointed to draw them up, and with some amendment the rules were adopted. The reports of the various lodges in the area Were received, and were considered. It was decided to hold the next meeting at St. Helens. Brother Morris Jones then gave an earnest address, counselling the members to renewed exertion, and 'reporting that the general position of the Order was very favourable. He trusted the future of the Con- vention would he a satisfactory one. This closed the business, and the company sat down to a good tea. A public open-air meeting was afterwards held, and there was a large attendance. Brother J. Brockhank, L.D., of St. Helens, presided, and gave an address; and Brothers J. Lindon, L.D. (St. Helens), and M. Jones. D.S. (Liverpool), also spoke. Brother John Taylor (Earlestown) sang "Have cour- age, my boy, to say 'No.'" The meeting concluded with thanks to the speakers and chairman, and a quantity of temperance literature was distributed.

DEATH OP A FORMER FRESCOT CURATE.—The Rev. Wißram Coombs, M.A. (late scholar of St. John's College, Cambridge), has just died at Oak Bank, Surbiton. Surrey, aged 74 years. On being ordained in 1838 by Dr. Sumner, Bishop of Chester, Mr. Coombs was licensed to the curacy of Prescot.- Lancashire. From here he was preferred in 1841 to the incumbency of St. Catherine s, Wigan, which he held till 1858. After holding appointments in Northumberland and Herts, he accepted in 1874 the vicarage of Christ Church, Douglas, or Parbold. or Wigan,-on the nomination of the Rev. John Spar- ling, M.A., the then Rector of Bccleston, near Ch or- ley. Mr. Coombs resigned this benefice some four years ago. The evidence, which was with respect to the conveyance of the Vyrnwy water pipes across the Weaver, was concluded, and the arbitrator, Sir Douglas Galton, C. 8., reserved his award. Mr. H. J. Tollemache. 31. P., has sent the followingletttr I 9 Mr. Charles Speakman, clerk to the Nantwich ,Board of Guardians:—" Dear Sir,—l am much, .obliged for the copy. of a. resolution passed by the Board of Guardians re Weaver Trust. The Weaver Trust has been most carefully administered by the- present managers, and entirely in the interest.of the county. Mr. Brunner's; proposal to alter the- management of the trust would probably be most disastrous from an official point of view, and his suggestion that the surplus funds should be de- voted to pay for the damage which he and other brine pumpers cause is a monstrous one." DEATH OF THE DOWAGER LADY GERARD. Lady Gerard, widow of the late Lord Gerard of Bryn, died on Friday week last, at Twyfoid Abbey, Ealing, where she had resently been residing. Her ladyship has for some years suffered much from ill- health, and consequently has been seldom able to take part in social events and public ceremonies, but the people of Ashton and district will have kindly remembrance of her goodness and charity during the years she resided at Garswood. Lady Gerard was the daughter of the late Mr. Edward Clifton, of Lytham Hall, and sister of Major Clifton Dicconson, of Wrightington. Mrs. Clifton succeeded to the estate of her mother, and took the name of Dicconson, and she was 'succeeded by her son, the late Mr. Thomas Dicconson, and then by the present , owner of the Wrightingtp estates. The deceased lady married the late Lord Gerard in 1849, when he was Mr. Robert Tolver Gerard. Five Tears later he I succeeded to the baronetcy, and in 1576 was raised to the peerage. The remains of the deceased lady were interred on Tuesday morning in Garswood Churchyard, where his lordship was buried. The ceremony was performed by the Roman Catholic Bishop of Liverpool, assisted by Canon Carr and a large number of priests.

Mr. Luke Holmes, auctioneer, of Runcorn, sub- mitted several lots of freehold property for public sale at Wilson's Hotel, Bridge-st., Runcorn, on Thursday evening, with a view to wind up a trust. Lot 1, freehold building in Bridge-st., and known as the Gospel Hall, with the out-offices and land be- longing thereto, the gross annual rental being £2O, was purchased by Mr. Prodsham for a client at £182; whilst lot 2. a chief rent of £4 3s, charged on I six dwelling-houses, yard, and premises in Mill-st.. now in the respective occupations of Joseph Ashworth, Thos. Mulger, John White, and others, as tenants, was knocked down at £67 103 to Mr. Dobson. Church-st. Lot 3, a chief rent of £5 19s, charged on three dwelling-houses, smithy, and other premises, situate in Mill-st., and now in the respective occupations as tenants thereof of Joseph Plant,' James Shaw, George Lewis, and, others, was purchased for £9O by Mr. Stein, who was also the highest bidder, and consequently the purchaser, of a chief rent of £lO 10s, charged on ten dwelling-houses and coal-bard, also situ- ate in Mill-st. and Brunswick-st., now in the respective occupations of Mary Rowley, J. Starkey, W. Barnes, and others, as tenants. The price realised for this lot was £205. Mr. Dugdale, butcher, of Church-st., purchased the next lot, which was a chief rent of £7 15s 6d, charged on three dwelling-houses and premises in Brunswick-st., now tenanted by Mrs. Armstrong, C. Littler, and Jona- than Pickstock, the price realised being £134. A chief rent of £2 13s on a house in Cooper-st., at present in the occupation of Mr. George Edwards, was also purchas'ed by Mr. Dugdale at £36. The whole of the chief rents are redeemable upon giving six month's notice, and by payment of 20 years' purchase. Messrs. Saunders, Nicholson, and Reeder, solicitors, of Wath-upon-Dearne, near Rotherham, and Messrs. Ford and Warren, solici- tors, o' 81, Albion-st., Leeds, looked to the interests of, the vendors.

THE WESLEYAN CONFERENCE. • The 145th annual session of the Wesleyan Coaference was opened at Wesley Chapel, Camborne, on Tuesday morning; the Rev. John Walton M.A., the retiring pre- sident, taking the ehair—Phe Secretary announced that there were eight vacancies in the Legal Hundred—four caused by death and 4by nomination. The next business was theelection of president. The result was as follows:— Rev. Joseph Bush, 218; Dr. Stephenson, 70; Rev. Chas. H. Kelly, 57.—The President's address was the first item on re-assembling in the afternoon. He thanked the Con- ference for the confidence manifested by the vote he had received, and said he would try to justify it. He named two factors which would greatly conduce to a successful conference—great freedom of speech and rigid economy of words. The pastoral address to the societies has been prepared by the Rev. George Bowden, and will be read in Conference when revised by a com- mittee, which was appointed. The next Conference is invited to Sheffield. The Rev. Thomas Allen, chairman of the Sheffield district, stated that a hearty welcome would be given and provision made for 400 ministers. The invitation was accepted. Several matters relating to the Wesleyan College were reported by the Rev. Thos. Allen and an influential committee appointed to consider them. The Conference thei? adjourned.

•The conference re-assembled on Wednesday morning, the chair being occupied by the newly-elected president. Most of the time of the session was occupied in adopt- ing a suitable official record of those ministers who have died during the year. The list included 35. The pro- posed amalgamation of English and Welsh circuits in South Wales will be considered by a committee. At the open session the public had the opportunity of attending the Conference. The object of the session was to wel- come representatives from affiliated conferences and to hear their addresses. The Rer.. Charles H. Kelly, who, as the representative of the English Conference has recently attended the general conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church of the United States, gave an address which evoked loud and frequent applause.— Dr. Stewart, of the New Brunswick Conference, Canada, was introduced to the conference. The Revs. Henry Bath, of Australia, and W. Morley, New Zea- land, were introduced, and as Mr. Bath had immediately to return home the address was delivered by the Reverend W. Morlev.—The Revs. H. Wallace, M`Mullen, G. Robinson, and R. M. Lee were the bearers of an address from the Irish Conference, in which there was a hope that the national union of Eng- land and Ireland would not be severed. The paragraph was greeted with applause.—On Thursday, the confer- ence was resumed, the Rev Joseph Bush in the chair. The resolutions ole the quarterly meeting of the first London district ofi the special arrangements to be made in the future for the Methodist Cathedral. City-road Chapel, were read. These arrangements include the appointment of 12 eminent minig,ers each year as speeial preachers for Sunday mornings.

A man named Sargeant was indicted at the Essex Assizes, on Wednesday, for the murder of his wife, under circumstances of horrible barbarity. He was found guilty without a moment's hesitation, and received sen- tence of death. ILLICIT Snms.—Detectives who have been on the watch for some days in Birininghamstate that they have discovered in a vault at the back of the premises of Messrs. Stephenson and Co., wine merchants, an un- licensed distillery. In it are two stills capable of turn- ing out 200 gallons of whisky per week. One of the stills was warm. The cellar contained 300 gallons of wash, 00 gallons of whisky partly prepared, and a quan- tity of sugar and past. The firm deny all knowledge of the distillery, saying that the vault was rented from them by a person named Thompson, and they cannot account for the fact that the gas used in the vault was either supplied through their meter or from pipes in their untenanted cellars not far away, CADBURY'S caution the public against adulterated Cocoas, sold as pure Cocoa, to which about 4 per cent. of Alkali and other agents are added, to give appa- rent strength to the liquor, by making it a dart colour. This addition may be detected by the scent when a tin is freshly opened. No Cocoa can be stronger than Cadbury's, which is guaranteed absolutely pure.—Advt.

MAINTENANCE CASE.—John Dutton was brought up on a warrant to show cause why he should not contribute to the maintenance of his wife, Mary Ann Dutton. It was stated that the prisoner, who had been ordered by the magistrates to pay his wife 58 per week, had con- tributed nothing to her maintenance since August in last year, and flaw owed £l2 10q. Prisoner said that he had been looking for work in Scotland during that period, but had been unable to obtain it.—The Chief Constable: If you were a decent man you would tot need to go out of Warrington for it.—The prisoner was further charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Kautsford- toad on the 27th of October, 1887. On the first charge he was sentenced to a month's imprisonment, and on the second to another month, with hard labour. MONDAY.—Before Aldermanliarrison and Councillor

John Pierpoint. frumous DRIVING —Joseph Caldwell, baker, Westfield- St., was fined 5s and costs, and Henry Nicholls, butcher, Horsemarket-st., lOs and costs for this offence.

A DESERTER FROM THE "KING'S OWN."—Patrick Gallaghan was charged with having deserted in August last year from the "King's Own" Regiment, sta- tioned at Dublin. He admitted the desertion, and was remanded to await escort. DESTITUTE ARTISANS.—Robert Grant, carpenter, and Charles Williams, bricklayer, was charged with sleeping in a house in course of erection in Thelwall-lane, on the previous night, they not having any visible means of subsistance. The second defendant said that he had worked at the house during the day and not having sufficient money for lodgings had slept there with Grant, whom he had met, and who also had no mfbney. The priseners were discharged. WEDNESDAT.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett and John Fairclough. DittnczENs'ssB.—MarT Simpson was brought up on a charge of having been arunk in Brooke-place, Latchford. She was discharged on promising to leave the town. FnAtmuLEwr Exusmnierr.—Williani Berry, alias Peter Holland, was charged with having fraudulently enlisted in the 3rd Battalion of the South Lancashire Regiment. The offence consisted in the prisoner having stated at the time of his enlistment that he had not previously served, when he had,been for some time in the Militia.—Ser- geant Craythorne from the Barracks, Orford, said that , he was instructed to give the prisoner a very bad charac- ter.—The Bench ordered the prisoner to go to gaol for two months, with hard labour.
A BEOGAR.—John Clarke, a tramp, was sent to gaol for seven days, with hard labour, for having asked alms in Bridge-st. on the previous afternoon. _._ _ _

DauNKENny.ss.—Samuel Dodson, charged with having been drunk, and with begging in Bridge-st., on the pre- vious night, was discharged on promising to leave the town.—For having been drunk in Buttermarket-st., on Wednesday night, and for hawking without a license, William Drury was sent to gaol for seven days' with hard labour.
CHEAP Looorsos.—Jesse Ditchfield was charged with sleeping in Bank Park the previous night. The case was dismissed. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison and Dr. Gornall.

A DRUNKEN MIINDICANT.—James Sullivan was brought up in custody on a charge of having been drunk, and of having asked alms' in Bridge-st., on the day previous. He was committed to prison for seven days, with hard labour.

Cansury CASES.—Frederick Lamb was, summoned for having ill-treated a mare, on the 14th inst, by working it while in an unfit state, and William Lamb was sum- moned for having caused the horse to be worked. In- spector Aplin, of the R.S.P.C.A., did not press the case, and the defendants were only ordered to pay the costs.- -William Cannington was summoned for having ill- treated a horse by working it while in an unfit state in Scotland-road, on the 18th inst. James Newton was summoned for having caused the animal to be so worked. Inspector Greatrex, of the R.S.P.C.A. (Wigan) proved the case. A severe penalty was not pressed for. Canning- ton was ordered to pay the costs; and Newton was ordered to pay Zs 6d and costs.—John Heywood was summoned for having, in Dallatn-lane, on the 18th inst, worked a mare that was totally unfit for work, thus ill- treating it. It was stated that the defendant was so poor as to be in receipt of parish relief ; and the magis- trates only ordered him to pay the costs of the summons, 3s 6d.

MASTER AND SEAVANT.—John Ratcliffe, a youth, was summoned by William Warburton, glass manufacturer. Napier-st., for having broken his contract of service on the 18th last, putting him to a cost of £2 las. In consequence Mr. Warburton was put to great incon- venience, and failed to get the order out in the required time.
