On Saturday. in the cricket match between Surrey and Middlesex, the former won by three wickets. In the match with the Australians, Sussex won by 58 runs. The match between M.C.C. and Notts ended in a. draw, and in the match with Kent Gloucestershire won by an innings and 44 runs. In the• Rounders National Shield semi-final tie, Cres- cent. v. Widnes, the resulkwas as follows :—Crescent, first innings, 37, second innings, 41; Widnes, first in- nings, 11, second ianin,gs, 10, third innings, 10. Warrington and Widnes Football Clubs have at last come to their sensw, and they intend "burying the hatchet" for ever. The above news will be gladly re- ceived by an Rugby enthusiasts in the West Lancashire district, as such two well-known exponents of the fav- ourite winter pastime to be at loggerheads was indeed a sad mistake.—A 100 Yards Match is reported to have taken place at Dakota, America, on the 4th instant, be- tween W. Hough and W. Pepper, when the first-named won in lOsec. It surely cannot be " Billy " Hough, of Warrington, who, before he left for the States, some years ago, was one of the best quarter runners in this district? Anyhow, he never showed anything like "evens" when on this side the water.— "Athletic News."

Rain interfered with the game between Warrington and Cheetham Hill on Saturday, and there is no doubt that the heavy shower which occurred during the in- nings of the Cheetham team added to their success. War- rington went to the wickets first, totalling 82, Tinsley being responsible for 26 and Crosfield 16, whilst C. G. Lawton made 20 (not out.) With the aid of Morgan tha , the remaining wickets put on the required number, and finally won eleven runs, viz., Cheetham Hill, 93; Warrington, 82.. Fleetwood took three wickets for 40, Lawton two for 17, and J. J. Crosfield three for 17. ..

Some 'tall scoring was witnessed on Tuesday, when the Australians, who were without the services of Blackham, made a total of 319, against Cambridge Past and Pre- sent. Bannennan scored 93, and carried his bat through the innings. Lancashire made a creditable performance in their encounter with Derbyshire, on Tuesday, at Old Trafford. Despite the softness of the ground, consequent on the rain, Lancashire, who had made 87 for the loss of one wicket on Monday, increased their score on Tuesday to 182. Being 95 runs to the bad, Derbyshire went in a second time, but were all cast in an hour forthe small score of 17 runs. Lancashire won by an innings and 78 runs. Briggs took six wickets for four runs. On the same day Surrey defeated Kent by 89 runs, • and Yorkshire were decisively victorious over Notts.
NO. 27.-CADISHEAD AND IRLAM.

Some Of the merely "incidental" works of the Ship Canal undertaking would, if they stood by themselves, be regarded as operations of no mean magnitude, but which, when placed in comparison with the main scheme—of which, as the name they are designated by implies, they are but incidents— sink into littleness. Of these larger subsidiary works perhaps none are of more importance than the deviation of the several railways which cross the intended track of the canal. We have already seen that at Warrington three important railways are to be deviated to some extent from their present route and carried over the new canal by viaducts at a considerable height. At Cadishead, orbetween Cadishead and Irlam, there are other two railways which it is proposed to deal with in the same way.

mile east of the offices at Morris Brook. The barrows are filled in the cutting, and one man is kept continually going up and down the planks, which are at an angle of about 45 degrees. From the top of the embankment to the bottom of the cutting measures about forty feet. The horse road gives the requisite power for drawing the barrow and man up the plank, and when the barrow has been emptied at the top, and loosened, the man,with the barrow behind him, slides down the plank again. It is stated that in this manner there are about 100 barrows-full of earth taken out in an hour. On this sec- tion there are six horse roads and two steam barrow roads. The latter have each a small engine from which power is supplied, and instead of the barrow being fastened to a rope there is a platform on which they are placed, sufficiently large to hold eight barrows. They take at least twice the time to go up the planks as do the horse barrows, and there is also some delay in loading and unloading. so that the average rate per hour only exceeds the horse roads by about 25. There is also on the cutting a steam travelling crane, with a gib of 50ft. girders. This is used for winding up the earth in buc- kets where there is water in the cutting. When the diversion of the river is completed a foot bridge will be cuilt across it, leading to a new road on the north side of the canal, which will go to Padgate. Thelwall-lane will be cut through, and a ferry provided on the canal sufficient to carry a load of fifteen tons across. The prin- cipal work on this section, besides the cutting, is the making of the locks a little to the west of Morris Brook, I and a railway deviation, which will render necessary the formation of embankments. THE FATALITY AT RIXTON. • •

An inquiry was held at Rixton on Montia:y, touching the circumstances of the death of a boy named Charles Whitfield, a greaser, who was employed on the works at Rixton. On the 19th instant he was run over by a wag- gon, sustaining injuries that rendered it necessary on the following day to amputate one of his legs. He did not long survive the operation. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased came by his death acci- dentally.

PROGRESS AT FLIXTON. Satisfactory arrangements have been made with the Barton Rural Sanitary Authority for the immediate pos- session of the Authority's sewage farm at Flixtod, which is situate within the line of the canal. By this arrangement the contractor will be able to proceed with a further length of the Flixton section, a start having al- ready been made at Hulme's bridge. The contractor has almost completed the stonework over the Bridgewater Canal at Barton, which is to form the new entrance into Trafford Park. A ballast line has been completed be- tween Mode Wheel and the locks at Barton. THE RAIN AND THE WORKS.—STOPPAGE AT

div.head: WARRINGTON AND STOCKPORT RAILWAY.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND STOCKPORT RAILWAY.

The first of these to be encountered by a person passing through Cadishead from Warrington, and in the direction of Manchester, is that which, branching off at some distance to the left trom the Liverpool and Manchester railway of the Cheshire Lines Cominittee,carries passengers and traffic from Liverpool and Warrington right through to Stock- port. This is known as deviation railway No. 4in the Ship Canal Act. The deviation of this line will begin at a point on the Cheshire side of the Mersey, about three-quarters of a mile in the further side of Partington station, and will termi- nate on the Lancashire side of the river, very close to the junction with the Liverpool and Manchester railway. From its commencement it will begin to rise on embankments by a gradient of 1 in 135, and it will cross the Mersey on a new bridge built for the purpose at an altitude of 72ft. lin, above the water level, and a little farther on it will pass over the canal on a specially constructed viaduct at a height of no less than 77 feet above •the intended water level. At this point, however, the canal waters will be at a considerably lower level than the natural level of the adjacent ground, and the I viaduct will consequently be only about 60 feet above the surtace of the earth. In cross- ing this viaduct the deviated line will have reached its highest point, and will thence begin to descend, by the same gradient ' of 1 in 13,5, till it rejoins the existing railway, as already stated, near the junction of the two lines. The new line, it should be explained, will be con- , , structed on the Warrington or western side of the old line. In its course the new line will touch upon some highways, the manner of dealing with which is duly specified in the Act of Parliament or delinea- ted in official plans. The road to the north of Par- tington, which runs at right angles with the rail- way, is one of those affected. This roadway, the level of which is to be unaltered, will, in the future, pass through the new railway embankment under an arch with a span of 25ft. and a height of 15ft. The main road which passes through Cadishead and leads from Warrington to Manchester will likewise have to be provided for, and the thoroughfare in this instance will be preserved by an under-bridge of 36ft. span and a height of 18ft. As in the other case the level of this road will not be altered. It is intended to construct, on the Manchester side of the new railway at Cadishead, a new road of no very great length to connect the Manchester and War- rington main road with another public road known as Moss-lane—lying to the left of a person going to- wards Manchester—and this having been done the Canal Company will have the power to stop up and extinguish all rights of way over so much of Moss- lane as lies between a house which is scheduled as being in the ownership of Mr. Ralph Unsworth and the railway. It may have been noticed that there are two railway stations—that at Partington and that at Cadishead—lying between the commence- ment and the termination of the deviation of rail- way just referred to. In future the Cadishead sta- tion, instead of being at the level, or indeed rather below the natural level, of the grounO., will have to be at the height of about 25ft. above the ground, for that is the height at which the embankment of the new railway will be at this point. Partington station will also be raised between 10ft. and 20ft. higher than it is at present. LIVERPOOL AND MANCHESTER RAILWAY. _ _

' Eastward from Cadishead and near to Lower Irlam is the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, from which, as we have mentioned above, the line to Stockport, the deviation of which we have been treating of, is a branch. This Liverpool and Man- chester Railway also crosses the intended course of the Ship Canal, and will also be slightly deviated from its present course and carried over the canal on a high viaduct. The deviation in this case will be- gin about one hundred yards on the Liverpool side of Flixton station, and will terminate some five or six hundred yards on the Liverpool side of Irlam s'Ation. In its course it will touch upon a bend of the Mersey, and will, in addition to crossing the canal, pass over the lrwell. The up and down gra- dients of the embankment of this deviation railway will, as in the former case, be as 1 in 13,5. At the point where the rails will cross the canal they will be 77 feet above the intended water level, and about 58 feet above the surface of the ground on either side of the canaLso that it will be seen that here the banks of the canal will rise little less than 20 feet above the surface of the water. To accommo- date this deviated line the Irwell will be spanned by a bridge about 67' feet above its water level, 'and in the future passengers from Warrington to Man- chester by this route will be cairied over the stream at that height. The road from Worsley to Warring- ton will have to be pasied by the new line, and its surface will be lowered by 20f 1. Gin, in order that it may run through the embankment and have an overbridge with a span of 36 feet and a height of 18 feet. It may here be mentioned that this new line of metals will run parall.l with and on the Cadishead side oi the old line, and further tl'at the old line will be abandoned after the new one has come into use. CONDITIONS. . . _

As might be expected, the Ship Canal Company are under some stringent conditions with regard to the work of deviating these two railways. We find from that part of their Act which is devoted to the "protection of the Cheshire Lines Committee," that before they in any way alter or interfere with the present lines and stations, they must complete new substituted stations, with suitable approaches, sid- ings, signals, and other works and conveniences. All bridges to be constructed by the Company for carry- ing any road, whether public or private, over either of the deviation railways, shall have a headway of not less than fourteen feet six inches from the level of the railway, and shall have a span of not less than fifty feet, measured on the square. All the works are to be executed at the expense of the Canal Com- pany, and under the superintendence, and to the reasonable satisfaction of the railway company's principal engineer. Further, it is provided that the works are to be constructed so as not to impede or interfere with the free and uninterrupted and safe use of the railways, and if any such obstruction take place, the Cans,l Company will forfeit to the Cheshire Lines Committee the sum of £lOO as ascer- tained damages for every hour or part of an hour during which the obstruction continues. During the construction of the works, the Canal Company will have to pay to the railway authorities all rea- sonable expense of employment by them of a suffi- cient number of inspectors or watchmen, for watch- ing the railways and works, and for preventing, as far as may be, all danger that may arise from any of the operations, or from the acts or defaults of the Com- pany or their contractors. _ _

EASTHAM.

An intereting point in the construction of the canal has been started at Eastham, where the laying of the stone" toe " of the estuary embankment at the mouth of the canal between the entrance to the locks and the Eastharn Ferry Pier has been commenced. The interest in the canal is still kept up, and every fine day boat loads of people are brought to visit this end of the canal. 'ACCIDENTS NEAR EASTFIAM.

The other evening, as a man named John Hamer, who lived in one of the huts at Pool Hall Brook, was leaving the hut he fell down dead. He was a mason, and was a native of Otley, Yorkshire. It is supposed that he was subject to heart disease. The fitter, Gambriel, who lost both his legs last March by an accident, has now left the hospital, and is enjoying gool health.

tfitLWALL. On the section extending from Latchford to Warbur- ton there are one German excavator. four steam navvies of the American type, and two Priestman's grabs, not to speak of the large number of locomotives that are kept so busily engaged. The wet weather has, however, greatly interfered with the operations. The busiest scene is at Thelwall and the neighbourhood. In addition to the steam navvies there are horse and steam barrow " roads at work on the diversion of the river, about a

div.head: BARTON.
div.p: BARTON.

On most of the section;-eilhe.. Ship Canal works the recent heavy, rains have greatly interfered with the pro- gress of the cuttings and other work. The men have in consequence had considerable "broken time," and there has not been so much advance as there would otherwise have been. Most inconvenience has been felt in the neighbourhood of Barton, where the river Irwell has overflowed its banks. On Tuesday night and early on Wednesday morning the rain came down in torrents, and the navvies were compelled to cPa se work. Footbridges "Across the river at Hulme's bridge and the Calamanca locks were immersed. The meadows at Salt Eye and below Croftsbank, where the Manchester Corporation propose constructing their sewage works, were covered with water. In some parts of the Skip Canal cutting the water is several feet deep, in consequence of which, at Stiggin's Island, where a depth of 40 feet has been reached, blasting operations have ceased for the pre- sent.

WORKMEN'S EXCURSION. The workmen in the employ of the Manchester Ship Canal Company (Bridgewater Undertaking), had their annual excursion to Liverpool on Saturday. Including the wives and families of the men, the excursionists numbered about 500, and the accommodation of the pad- dle steamer Dagmar was severely taxed to find room for them. After a most pleasant sail the party were landed at Liverpool about half-past twelve, and the afternoon was spent in viewing the sights of the city or by a visit to New Brighton, while the attractions of the Ship Canal Works lured not a few to Fa stham. Runcorn was safely reached about half-past ten at night, all having spent a most enjoyable day, asthe weather was beautifully fine. The Volunteer Band accompanied the excursion and ad- ded much to the pleasures of the day by their admirable music.

A BRIGHT FORECAST. Mr. Manisty, Aurveyor of the Ship Canal, at a dinner of the National Association of Master Builders at Liver- pool on Wednesday night, slid it was no small under- taking to take ocean-going fteamers right into the heart of England. He thought that great skill had been shown by the engineer of the Manchester Ship Canal in draw- ing up his glans, and extraordinary organising power had been also shown on the part of the contractor. He believed that very soon the promoters of that scheme would be standing alongside their docks in Manchester, seeing these big ocean-going steamers coining abreast of those magnificent docks. He was speaking to an assem- blage of architects, engineers, and surveyors, who hadno animus in the matter, but who merely looked at the scheme as a gigantic one, which was to help to keep England in the proud position of the foremost nation in manu- facturing in the world ; and if anything could be done to keep her in that position by English engineers, he was sure it would have the sympathy of all present. The Manchester Ship Canal would be larger than any canal that had .ever been constructed. It would have a width of 120 ft. at the bottom, and 26ft. of water all the way up to Manchester, so that the largest steamer afloat would be able to go up to Manchester. Those connected with the scheme were the men who would carry it through. They had great faith in their leaders, and he believed that the canal would be the inauguration of a great amount of work for engineers and contractors all over the world.

div.head: FASHIONABLE MARRIAGE.
div.p: FASHIONABLE MARRIAGE.

On Monday afternoon, in St. Paul's Church, Knightsbridge, the wedding took place of Mr. F. G. Hodgson R hefts, only son ot the late Mr. 11. and Mrs. Armstrong Roberts, of 11, Kensington Gore. with Miss Violet Cunliffe, eldest daugh:er of Mr, and Mrs. Ellis Brooke Cunliffe, of High Legh Knutsford, and 18, Ennismore Gardens, Kensington, S.W. The service was fully choral, and the officia- ting clergy were the Rev. John Spading, of Petton Park, grandfather of the bride, and the Rev. H. Montague Villiers, M.A., vicar of St. Paul's. The bride, who was given away by her father, was attired in a thick white corded silk with very long train, the front covered with flounces of point de gaze and thick soft ruches of white ostrich feathers. She wore a few sprays of orange blossoms in her hair, and a very long tulle veil fastened with a diamond star. Her other ornament was a diamond, pearl, and turquoise necklace, both articles being the gifts of the bride- groom. Her bouquet was of exotics. Miss Cunliffe was attended by four charming bridesmaids, attired in Directoire coats of tan-coloured cloth over pink moire, with pink moire sashes; and they also wore tan-coloured hats trimmed with pink carnations. Each carried a beautifully painted pink fan and a bouquet of pink carnations tied with tan ribbons, all the gift of the bridegroom. The bridesmaids were Misses Veronica, Vanda, and Verbena Cunliffe, sisters of the bride, and Miss Lue Hodgson Roberts, sister of the bridegroom. Mr. Greenall acted as groomsman. A pleasing feature was introduced in the wedding by the household servants, who lined the aisle of the church. The reception took place at Mr. Ellis Cunliffe's town residence, and among the ' invited guests were the Dowager Duchess of Albans, Lord and Lady Braye, the Right Hon. Vis- count and Viscountess Cross, Lord and Lady Ellen- borough, Sir Humphrey and Lady de Trafford, lion. Mrs. Burgess, Sir Thomas and Lady Aleyrick, Sir Thomas and Lady Dyer, Sir Robert and Lady Cun- liffe, Lady Alexandrina Cunliffe, Mrs. Arinstrong Roberts, Mrs. Hodgson, Mr. Ellis Sperling Cunliffe, Mr. J. Brooks Cunliffe, Miss Valentia Cunliffe, Miss Virginie Cunliffe, Sir Henry and Lady Beddinfeld, General Sir Edward Hamley, M.P., General Sir James and Lady Hilda Johnes, Sir Ralph and Lady Blois, Lady Ina Durrant, Baron and Baroness de Longueil, Rustem Pasha, Mr. and Lady Georgina Peel, the Hon. Mr. and Mrs. Orde Powlett, &c. Later in the afternoon Mr. and Mrs. Hodgson Roberts left for Switzerland to pass the honeymoon. Among the numerous and costly preeents were a brougham, a pair of splendid horses, and a quantity of silver from a lady, and a very handsome clock from the household servants.

GREAT FIRE.--By a fire which occurred on Thursday in one of the Sandon Dock sheds, Liverpool, about 4,000 bales of cotton and 1,000 tons of Indian corn were totally destroyed.. The damage to the stock and shed is roughly estimated at £70,000. div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

"A Country House" is the title of a story from the pen of Mrs Herbert Martin, author of "Bonnie Lesley." It is issued in the "Girls' Own Favourite Library," the series by 6lessrs. Griffith, Farren, and Co., and deserves to be a favourite of its class. It is written in a cheerful, healthy strain, and teaches wholesome lessons in a most attractive way. The characters are distinctly and firmly drawn, and their fortunes are therefore followed with interest. Mary, the "Country Mouse," is a loveable creature, and a bright example to her sex. The volume is well printed, handsomely bound, and admirably il- lustrated. In the Great Writers series for July (published by Mr. Walter Scott) we have the "Life of Johann Wolfgang Goethe," by Mr. James Sime. It need hardly be said that a well-written biography of the greatest poet and thinker which Germany has pro- duced is interesting and profitable reading. There is plenty of room for difference of opinion as to Goethe's writings and their tendency, and this being the case, there is all the more need for such a dispas- sionate record of the maiirfacts of his career as Mr. Sime presents. "Faust "is such a trulygreat work that his biographer has done well to deal at length with its inception, evolution, and execution. As we have it, it was the work not of a year, but of a life time.

The "Poems of Ossian is a welcome addition to the Canterbury Poets. They constitute no small part of the classic literature of Scotland; and will ever remain an interesting monument of the labours of Mr. James Macpherson. It was paving him too great a compliment, however, to suppose that he was the author of the poems—just as Chatterton imposed upon his contemporaries with the Rowley manuscripts. It may now be said to be placed be- yond doubt that all that Mr. Macpherson did was to collect, translate, and collate, lie certainly did write verse on his own account; but it was in the stilted style of the last century, and in utter con- trast to the fervour, tire, and simplicity of the Songs of Ossian. The volume contains an historical and critical introduction by Mr. George Eyre-Todd, who has spared no pains to do justice to the memory. of Mr. Macpherson while putting the general reader a position to understand and appreciate the merits of the poems of Ossian. No library, even of the smaller kind, can be said to be complete without this volume.

The Autobiography of Lord Herbert of Cherbury reaches us in the Camelot series. It is a thoroughly readable work, and will be relished when the philosophical works of the great Diest lie untouched upon the shelves. There is not a little of quaint conceit as well as of solid sense in the autobiography, while at the same time it is a picture of the man- ners and customs of the seventeenth century. Lord Herbert was the eldest brother of "holy George Herbert ; " it was a remarkable family to produce two brothers so greatly distinguished. "Jack Dudley's Wife," is another issue from the teeming press of Mr. Walter Scott. The story is by E. M. Davy, and originally appeared in the "New- castle Weekly Chronicle." Its success appears to have been considerable; hence its reproduction in book form. Jack Dudley's Wife is an uncommon creature, and the reader is interested in her from the first introduction. The story has a plot and a oecret, which together sustain the interest of the reader. It is not a novel of the highest rank, but it is one that does not at any rate become tiresome. As it is issued in clear large type, it is very suitable for railway reading. Disease; its Prevention and Cure by Simple Natural Means," is the title of an interesting pam- phlet by Mr. C. G. Godfrey. A number of facts are adduced in this little work which go to support Mr. Godfrey's theory, which is, that people would be stronger and healthier, and therefore better able to resist disease, if they would take more exercise. more salt, and keep pretty well to dry food. He be- lieves with Hippocrates that "it is nature that cures disease."

The current issue (part 21) of the History of Lan- cashire, which is being published by Mr. John Hey- wood, commences the record of the borough of Sal- ford. There is a fine plate of the Manchester As- size Courts; a view of the Manchester Exchange erected in 1729; another of the Exchange of 1806; and a third of the Royal Exchange completed in /874.

We have received the first of two supplements which the " Graphic " is issuing—one to-day, and the other next Saturday. They illustrate the beauti- ful scenery of the English Lake District. The views are very faithful and remarkably well executed, and are, therefore, likely to be treasured. The "Church Monthly,' edited by Mr. F. Sher- lock, has always something interesting, and it is capitally illustrated. It is admirably adapted for parish localisation.
MR. GLADSTONE'S GOLDEN WEDDING.

Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone on Wednesday reached the fiftieth anniversary of their wedding day, and re- ceived numerous telegrams and letters of congratu- lation, as well as presents. It was on July 25, 1830, at Ilawarden Church, that the marriage of the right honourable gentleman and his esteemed lady took place. Numerous letters of congratula- tion from political bodies were received. At Spencer House, St. James, London, theresidence of' the Earl and Countess Spencer, Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone were pre- sented with their portraits. painted by Frank Hall and Professor Herkomer, and a set of massive silver vases. The presentation took place in the large drawing room, among those present being Sir George Trevelyan, Mr. J. Morley, Mr. Shaw-Lefevre, Lord Rosebery, Mr. Childers, Mr. Mundella, Lord Herschel', Lord Aberdeen, Lord Kimberley, Sir William Harcourt, Mr. Campbell- Bannerman, Lord Kensington, Mr. Stansfield. Sir Ughtred Kay Shuttleworth, , and Mr. Grant Duff. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone drove up in an open carriage at noon, Mr. Gladstone wearin,,c, a light dust coat, and white tower in his button-hole. He looked exceedingly well, and received hearty hand shakes as he entered Spencer House. Mrs. Glaclstone,wore a white bonnet, and over her shoulders a beautiful white lace shawl, which, it is understood, was used at her wedding. On entering the room where the people were assembled, Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, who were accompanied by MISS Gladstone and their grand-son,.were received with a hearty welcome. Mr. Gladstone, in acknowledging tht presentation, said he hoped he might be allowed to en- dorse the references in the address presented to Mrs. Gladstone, as being absolutely true. It was difficult for him to give an adequate idea of the domestic happiness which he had 'enjoyed during the past fifty years. To this extent he concurred entirely with the terms of the address. When it came to allusions to himself, difficulty I arose, for he could not help but feel that many words used were of two flattering -a character. Referring to Ithe long time he had been in public life, he said his con- duct had often`been criticised, sometimes, perhaps, un- justly, bet he could not help feeling that on the whole 'their criticisms had been more to his benefit than the re- verse. At all events, he could say that in the whole of that long retrospect he could hardly recall in his public life any incident painful to his recollection. He thanked them.very warmly for the presentation. Mrs. Gladstone I also said a few words of thanks.

MR. GLADSTONE AT THIRTY. "The British Senate in 1838," now a scarce book, con- tains an early portrait of Mr. Gladstone. It is one of those collections of personal sketches in the ,House of Commons which wicked people even in these days write, and are occasionally remonstrated with for the impro- priety of the act. But out of these few sketches of fifty years ago one gets a clearer notion of men and things than out of more pretentioustomes. Here is what it says 'about Mr. Gladstone at the very beginning of his politi- cal career :—" Mr. Gladstone's appearance and manners are much in his favour. He is a fine-looking man. He is about the usual height, and of good figure. His coun- tenance is mild and pleasant, and has a highly intellec- tual expression. His eyes are clear and quick. His ,eye- brows are dark and rather prominent. There ris not a dandy in the House but what envies what Truefit would call his fine head of jet black hair.' It is always care- fatly parted from the crown downwards to his brow, where it is tastefully shaded. His features are small and regular, and his complexion must AN a very Unworthy witness if he does not possess an abundant stock of health."

div.head: CHRISTIAN FAMILY.
div.p: A CHRISTIAN FAMILY.

A writer two years ago sold :—Nothing impressed me more at Hawarden than the beautiful sympathy exist. ing between all the members of Mr. Gladstone's family. Theirs appears to be an ideal, Christian home--a family. loving God and loving each other. In. marrying marrying into the Glynnes, speaking of them as a family,Mr.Gladstone clearly did the very best thing for the development of his character. Knights, scholars, theologians, the Glynnes seem to have been a benevolent and spiritual-minded race, and Mrs. Gladstone, through herself and through her children, gives evidence that their best qualities have not become extinct with the death of the last of the male line, her brother, Sir Stephen Glynn. Her son, Stephen, a sweet-faced, modest man, is rector of the parish; her daughter, Mrs. Drety, is wife of her son's curate. She herself maintains an orphanage within the grounds of Hawarden. One might argue from the character .of the family to the character of its illustrioss head. They take the most minute and eager interest in the great question in which Mr. Gladstone is now engaged. "It is a great disappointment to us," said Miss Helen Glad- stone to the guests at her table at luncheon," that Mrs. Drew cannot be down with us to-day. She is the most ardent Home Ruler of us all." Mrs. Drew, unhappily, was ill upstairs. But she sent down a message later that she hoped everybodYwould carry away a flower from the table, as her gift to the deputations.

The MAYOR read the notice convening the meeting, -and the resolution passed at the last meeting of the Council directing that the statement showing the quan- tities of material and manufactures, with the cost, &c., should be prepared, and proceeded to say that as that was an adjourned meeting, it would only be competent for them to discuss the statement made by Alderman Burgess at the last meeting, and the resolution then passed; and afterwards to pass any resolution bearing on such remarks or the statement presented. It was for the gentleman who spoke last at the previous meet- ing to open the proceedings, but before that was done he wished to say he had received a letter from Councillor John Platt, dated that day, expressing his sorrow that he should not be able to attend the meeting of the Coun- cil thronli Councillor Mosss said he moved the adjournment at the last ineetin„cr, and in'approaching the subject again he wished to refer to an unpleasant element which he thought had crept in. He should not have referred to it had it not been for the remarks made by the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee, but as far as he was concerned he had no personal feeling in the matter, and he would take good care that he imported no personal feeling into it. liear, hear.) If anybody else chose to do so it was their own business and not his, but at the same time he did not think that should be any prevention to 'discussing freely and frankly anything that came before them. It was a public question and ought to be discussed as a public question without any referente to the persons who constituted the committee, and in anything he might say with reference to what he might call the historical part of the statement of Alder- man Burgess he Old not wish to be disrespectful to Alder- man Burgess or to the committee. That portion was purely historical, and did not come within his concep- tion of the position of the Sanitary Committe with refer- ence to that Council. He next came to the figures,which he proposed to show were not quite correct. Ald . Burgess's first statement was that had the old midden system beet), in force to-day it would have cost £8,882 ns 201, but he (Councillor Monks) did not know where the alderman got the figures from. Certainly they could not be based upon the experience they had in the old days when the midden system was in existence, because in 1879, when he was asked to speak on the financial aspect of that subject, he gave figures show- ing that instead of the old midden system being any loss whatever to the town, there was a profit of at least aid per closet on the transaction. But taking even the highest cost of collection then, it was exceeded under the new system, wkich had run up, he was very sorry to say. to a considerable sum, and even then it did not amount to the figures which the alderman had given them. He found that in 1879 the cost of collectionand manufacture was only 9s old per closet, and if it cost that to-day— and he saw no reason why it should not—the 8:341 closets would only cost £3,779 lOs 3d, so that he failed to see where the chairman got his figures from. Alderman Burgess's further state- ment showing how a saving was to be effec- ted would vanish unless he could prove that the cost of the collection on the old system would amount to the figures he quoted. There was one thing in connec- tion with the figures £6,483 which he was sorry to see, because the figures indicated not a further reduction in the cost of manufacture and improvement in the income at the Longford works, which he noticed with some sat- isfaction had been the case last year; but it was a fur- ther increase in expenditure and a very small increase in the income. With reference to Alderman Burgess's statement about the machinery being the very best, all he had to say was that he was not going to controvert the alderman's opinion. He presumed it was the best according to Alderman Burgess's opinion, but if he (Councillor Monks) did not attach the same importance to it he did not think there was any cause of offence in that. He judged it by its results as compared with the promises held out to the Council when they were induced to consent to the expenditure. With reference to the Rural Sanitary Authority, he did not suppose anyone would question that the system had abated a nuisance at Longford, and to that extent it might claim a fair amount of success. Whether it could have been done in any other way he was not at that moment prepared to say. The other remarks of Alderman Burgess did not touch upon the question which he (Councillor Monks) was concerned about ; but there was one remark which Mr. Crosfield made at the last meeting, and that was that they were taking steps to get the best information they could as to whether something could not be done by the aid of chemistry. They all knew chemistry had made very great strides during the last 20 years. and he did not see why chemistry should not be called in to deal with that subject; and he was in hopes it would be, and that thereby the cost of manufacture would be reduced. Mr. Crosfield also went on to say that it was net safe for a borough to be in such a condition, owing to the want of duplicate machinery. He had his own opinion about that and he thought it was very . .

likely that the present machinery had no attained to its maximum production, and until that point was reached Epe, for one, should certainly hold off from any further „ e4penditure for many rea.sens' and he was inclined to Vennk that the management at Longford was not what it Ehei..ld be—(hear, hear)—and it rested with the commit- tee be put that matter straight and see how far good, etipte, management at Longford, and perhaps other de-

partments, might bring about a better state of things which would obviate any further expense for years to come. With reference to the remarks about that system not costing the ratepayers much, they would all have their own opinions. He had prepared a statement show- ing what had been the cost from 1879, when it was first introduced, down to the 25th March last. He vouched for the accuracy of the figures, because they were taken entirely from the Borough Treasurer's reports which had been issued year after year, and from the reports of the Sanitary Committee issued on July 10th, 1279, and on the Bth November, 1884. Mr. Monks then distributed printed copies of the statement he had- prepartdo which was as follows The reports of the Sanitary Committee, dated 10th July, 1879, and 28th November, 1884, indicated very considerable saving in the working and management Of the nightsoil andLongford departments, and the (bun- cil consented to the necessary outlay accordingly, with the following results : s. d. It seemed to him that befell) they were asked to consent to further expenditure, which had al- ready exceeded £20,000-a any !arge amount--they ought to have a due regard to the rates, because all the money would have to be paid out of the rates, and a very large number of the ratepayers found it a pretty considerable burden to meet any additional rates which ' were required. They ought to be thoroughly well satis- fied that the existing machiaery was well managed, and that it had attained, or nearly attained, to its maxi- mum production, and then they would need to be thoroughly satisfied that the necessity existed for an ex- tension, and that the extension to be proposed *as the best for dealing with the material they had to deal with. Another thing, that he thought that they should require was that there should be more information given to the Council from month to month in reference to this matter. Seeing that the expenditure was a very large one-the expenditure of the Sanitary Committee, he thought, was practically more than one-half of the rates, or, at any rate, it formed a large proportion-he thought that information not only as to income, but as to expenditure, and to the quantity of material sent to Longford and dealt with, would be exceedingly valuable to the Council when considering any question that might arise in the future. He thought that the Sanitary Committee should explain how it was that the income had fallen so much below what was estimated in 1884, and how it was that the cost of the department had gone up so much. His own feeling was, and had been-based upon their experience of the early history of this question-that they could not do it for much less than it was done for up to that time. He found from figures that the actual loss to the Corporation for the last year had been £3,744, instead of £l,OOO as estimated, and from the figures that the Alderman gave them at the last meeting it was clearly to be expected that the expenditure for the com- ing year would be at least £.529 in access of last year, and that the income would be about £l9O over last year. So that they were in, altogether, for an excess next year of about £358 9s Od, instead of there being a further re- duction. He thought that these were matters that were open to criticism, and it was due to the Council that the Sanitary Committee should give some explana- tions. If his . figures were not true, the Committee would be able to disprove them. Mr. Monks then referred to " a second statement that he had prepared which was to the effect that he did not expect that, with a constantly increas- ing population, the cost of dealing with the refuse should remain at the same amount in 1888 as for 1884. He wsuld give the results of the past two years at so much per closet. The number of closets, December, 1883,was 7,537. If they took the expenditure for the year ending 2.5 th March, 1884, at £5,443 16s 7d, they found that the cost of collection and manufacture was 14s Sid, and the amount received for the same year at 3s 6d per closet, leaving a net loss of 10s 11id per closet.

Or, to put it in another way, instead of an estimated saving of 9s 2d (being the saving of £3,457 13s sd) per closet, they had for 1887 an increase of as 4d per closet, and for 1388 a reduction of is 11id only, and for the two years they had had the plant at work, an increase of 2id per closet instead of a saving of 9s 2d per; closet. The net cost in 1879, worked out on the same basis, was 4s sid per closet, so that it practically came to this, that they spent £20,719 15s 9d to increase the cost of dealing with their refuse from 4s sid to 85 11id per closet, and they would be asked to increase this capital outlay in order to put the plant and machinery in better condition to deal with it. The fact was the expenditure had been under-estimated about 40 per cent, the income had been over-estimated about 54 per cent, and the actual capital expenditure over the estimated expendi- ture came to about 39 per cent. They, as representa- tives of the ratepayers, had a perfect right to inquire into expenditure, and into anything else that had refer- ence to this question. Mr. Monks afterwards referred to the condition of the machinery at Longford, and ex- pressed his disbelief in the wisdom of dual control.

Alderman BURGESS said that the tone of Mr. Monks's observations had been of so satisfactory a character that no one could take exception to the way in which he had brought the question before the Council. It might be that he did not agree with him in all particulars; in the main particulars that he had brought before them he should be entirely at variance with Mr. Monks. If, how- ever, he could get anything from the figures that would help him and, the committee in doing what was a serious and difficult duty, he should avail himself of them, and feel grateful to Mr. Monks. He had always felt, and did now, that the duty of a Sanitary Com- mittee ' was to take care, to the best of their judgment and ability, of the health and the comfort of the people over whom they had oversight. If they had discharged their duty as a Sanitary Committee to the satisfaction of the Council, and to the satisfaction ' of the inhabitants of the borough, if they thought that they had not neglected their duty, and that they had brought to bear upon their duty a lively and intelligent mode of action, he submitted that they had done what was required of them. When he told them that the death rate in Warrington had been reduced in the time that this work had been going on from 31 to 21 in the 1,000, if they had succeeded to that extent he told them with all respect that he should not consider other mat- ters, while undertaking as for as possible to make the best use they could of the materials that were placed at their disposal in consequence of their having adopted a system for the improvement of the health of the inhabitants, which had such a beneficial result. He submitted that they had the best of machinery, and referred at length to a supplementary report of the visit of a deputation to other towns in regard to the sanitary system. He was I then proceeding to explain the basis upon which he cal-

culated what would have been the present costof the mid- den system as compared with the present system, when he remarked that to go into the figures would take too much time, and he would therefore hand his documents to the reporters. [The documents reached us too late last night to be given in full, bat we note that they consist mainly of detailed estimates, showing that, if the night- soil collection and disposal were now in force, as in 1870, the cost would be : Say £8,882 18s. Bd.

The above are the results of old and new systems of night-soil collection and disposal, showing a present pro- fit of £2,799 18s 8d in favour of the new system, and which sum is capable of being increased.) Proceeding. Mr. Burgess said that they had been trying experimental measures to get more out of the materiaa, but they could not get what they were entitled to. But was anyone else getting it? they were none of them getting more out of their material than they were at Longford. After further remarks on this point, Mr. Burgess denied that the machinery was in the condition that Mr. Monks had described it as being in. With reference to dual management, or interference on the part of the Borough Surveyor, he was sorry to say that the surveyor had been dragged up to Longford in a way that he had no right to be. This, he gave it to be under- stood, was the fault of the management, and he then criti- cised in severe terms the action of the manager. Alder- man Burgess was proceeding with his remarks, when Alderman HARRISON called attention to the fact that there was no quorum.

Councillor eARXER said that be had thought of mov- ing the adjournment of the meeting, as two or three members were absent who wished to say something on the matter. The Mayon thought that the pros and cons of the mat- ter had been fairly put before them. _

Councillor MoNirs.said that Alderman Burgess avoided the question of expenditure. Alderman BURGESS replied that the time had not come for him to take that question up; at an early period they would be right in challenging him and requiring an explanation on every point connected with the ex- penditure. _

The Mayon said that he was glad that they had the explanation given by Mr. Monks and Alderman Burgess. The Council then rose, but as the members were leav- ing the room Councillor JOHN PIBRPOIRT was heard to intimate that the members of the Sanitary CommitteA had gone out of the room in order to shirk the question; that was very disgraceful. The MAYOR : You are perfectly at liberty to think as you like, but I cannot give you any information.
Councillor JOHN PDZiiPOII.4 : I have it.from a member of the committee that he received notice to leave the the room—to which he otijected. The other members left.
The subject then dropped, and the meeting termina- ted.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, 'JULY 28, 1888.
THE ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER AT LATCHFORD. •

At Chester Assizes, on Thursday, Michael Garner (24), labourer, was indicted for the manslaughter of Anthony Gibbons, at Latchford, on the 12th of May last. Prisoner was also Charged on the coroner's inquisition. Mr E. Burke-Wood appeared for the prosecution, and the prisoner was defended by Mr J. E. Bankes. It appeared from the prosecution that the prisoner had been engaged as a labourer by Mr Hewitt, of Lower Wash Farm, Latchford, for about two yeats. The deceased Gibbons had been employed there also for a short time, and they had lived on very good terms. On the day in question they both left the farm and proceeded to the Rail- way Tavern, Latchford, in the evening. Gibbons at that time was the worse for drink, and was not supplied with drink, whilst the prisoner was. Sub- sequently it transpired that prisoner and the deceased had a quarrel, and in consequence of that deceased was ejected from the premises by the landlord. On the following morning, when Mr. Hewitt was in the yard, the deceased and prisoner were there. Deceased told Mr. Hewitt that they had had a row, and that the prisoner both kicked and struck him. Prisoner hearing that, replied, "I did not kick him; I hit him on the nose. He wanted to take some money out of my pocket." In a few days afterwards Gibbons died, but previously he made a statement. He said he was a native of Castlebar, Ireland, and that prisoner had knocked him down, and when on the ground he was kicked in the stomach about three times. Medical evi- dence was given to the effect that death resulted from rupture of the bladder, probably the result of a violent blow. Mr. Bankes addressed the jury on behalf of the prisoner, urging that it was likely deceased had sustained injury by falling and com- ing in contact with some projection. Prisoner was found not guilty.

div.head: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY.
div.p: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY.

The half-yearly meeting of Parr's Banking Com- pany, Limited, was held yesterday at noon, at the Bank premises, Winwick-et., Warrington. The chair was occupied by the managing director, Mr. J. Charl- ton Parr, and there was a good attendance of direc- tors and shareholders.—Mr. Jourr Dux (manager) read the half-yearly report, which stated that the profits for the half-year, after providing amply for all bad and doubtful debts, were very satisfactory. They recommended that an interim dividend at the Mite of £l5 per cent per annum be paid, free of income tax, and payable on and after the 31st July. There remained a considerable balance to be carried forward to the next account. The directors als6 mentioned that branches had been opened at Seaforth and Rainhill.—The CHAIR- mix said that he felt assured that he need not remind those present that that was only the half-yearly meeting, at which there was no production of balance sheet or ex- amination of figures. He was extremely happy th endorse what was contained in the report as to the business and position of the bank, which continued to be in every way satisfactory. He might also pay that the dividend that they were asked that day to declare had been well and fully earned, and that after its payment they had still a considerable sum to carry forward to the next annual account. The only other information which was vouch- safed in the directors' report was the opening of two sub- branches, one at Rainhill and one at Seaforth. They were merely branches for the convenierice of their cus- tomers, and for the protection of their business. He pro- posed that the report be adopted.—Mr. ECEERSLEY se- conded the motion, which was carried unanimously.—Sir GILBERT GREENALL proposed that the meeting sanction ithe payment of an interim dividend at the rate cf 15 per cent, per annum, as recommended by the directors.—The proposition was seconded by Captain WITIIINGTON, and carried.—Mr. H. NEILD proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman, and said that he felt assured that the share- holders must be gratified by the information that they had received regarding the prosperous condition of the bank.—The motion was seconded by tha Rev. W. H. WILLIAMS, and carried, after which the meeting ter- minated.

NAVAL MANOETIVRES.—The progress of the naval manceuvres was marked on Wednesday by the first in- teresting movements after the official declaration of war" between the fleets commanded respectively by Admirals Baird and Tryon. The latter lying in Bantry Bay—being blockaded there by Admiral Baird's squad- ron, which sailed from Milford on Sunday—kept the op- posing fleet pretty well employed throughout the day in watching the proceedings of the fast cruisers, but the ships returned to the anchorage at night without any change in the position of affairs. .

THR.EATENING MR. GLADSTONE.—A. German agent named Francis Egon Clotton, in business in Liverpool, was brought before the Deputy Stipendiary Magistrate on Thursday, and charged with having threatened to mur- der the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone. The prisoner, it seemed, had written a pamphlet and sent the original manuscript to Mrs. Gladstone, asking if he might dedi- cate the works to her. Unfortunately, the manuscript was lost or mislaid, and the prisoner was informed of that fact. -Labouring under the impression, however, that it was neither lost nor mislaid, but withheld, he wrote to Mr. Gladstone threatening that the righthonour- able gentleman "should not see the day of his golden wedding, far less the day when Home Rule should pass in the British Parliament, if the manuscript were not im- mediately returned." A TRADESMAN'S FINANCIAL DIFFICULTIES. A COMMITTAL ORDER SET ASIDE. .

At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. T. P. E. Thomposon, judge Mr. J. P. !Kearns appeared on behalf of Richard Seddon, hay and straw dealer. Baldwin-st.. St. Helens, to ask his Honour to allow an order of commitment againa, Frederick Coogan, described as a manager for Mr. E. Johnson! grocer, Runcorn. and formerly a grocer and provision dealer, at St. Helens, to stand. Mr. H. L. Riley appeared on behalf of Coogan.—Mr. Mearns said that at the last sitting of the court his Hon- our was satisfied, and an order for commitment was made. In his (Mr. Mearns's) absence an improper ap- plication was made to have the order set aside on the ground that the defendant could not get to the court in time, whilst the fact was that the defendant never in- tended to come to court. He would submit that the order ought to stand.—Mr. Riley said that everything done in that court, not done by Mr. Mearns, seemed to be improper. His Honour was not appealed to on the ground stated, but the defendant asked Mr. Kirkham, an agent, to appear for him and he was too late. It was partly on account of the negligence of the agent that his Honour set aside the order.— Mr. Mearns said the plaintiff had a claim against the de- fendant for £9 18s 9d, and he had paid no portion of it. He called a hurried sale, and disposed of his goods, realis- ing about £lOO. So far as the plaintiff knew, he had paid none of his creditors.—The plaintiff was called, and he said the defendant was earning about 28s per week. It would be about three months since he got the £lOO, and he had been working since.—ln reply to Mr. Riley, plaintiff said he knew the defendant had four children to keep, but he did not know what he had done with the £loo.—Mr. Riley submitted there was no case upon which his Honour could proceed. there was no evidence, and there had been no reasonable interval after the judg- ment for it to be satisfied.—Defendant was called, and in cross-examination by Mr. Mearns, he said he had a pretty good stock, but he did not think it proper to have a hur- ried sale. He was not advised to sell it. He did not put the money in his pockets, but paid it as far as it would go. The sale realised £93, and beyond that he had neither money in the house, bank, building societies, nor any other security. He only re- ceived £36 17s 2d from the sale and the other went in costs, and he was perfectly satisfied with what he re- ceived. Of that sum he paid £l2 2s ed for rent, and £7 to a friend, who lent him money.—Mr. Riley said this cross-examination was outside the question, that his Honour had to try. The question was whether, after judgment was signed, he had the means to Pay.— Defendant, in reply to further questions by Mr Mearns, said he might owe about £3OO, but he had no means to pay any of the creditors, He had not been discharged by Mr. Johnson for misconduct, but on account of another person not telling ,the troth about him.—Mr. Mearns asked his Honour to allow the order to start. That was a sort of thing which was too common in St. Helens. People defrauded creditors and never intended to pay.—His Honoursa,id he would make a new order of es per month with leave for the plaintiff to apply for more if the circumstances of the defendant improved.

div.head: HART V. THORNTON CASE.
div.p: THE HART V. THORNTON CASE.

At a sitting of the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before His Honour Judge Ffoulkes, Mr. Percy Davies, solicitor, made application for the payment out of court of Os., paid by the plain- tiff on issuing interrogatories. Mr. Davies stated that the case was one in which the plaintiff sued the defendant for certain certitlcates,.and the action was commenced in the High Court in London. It was, however, remitted from that court to the j County Court, and was heard by His Honour in October, 1887. judgment being then given for de- fendant with costs. The costs were, however, afterwards taxed by the learned Registrar, and allowed at .C 54 17s. 2d. Although plaintiff, in an affidavit filed in the course of the action, had sworn that he was in receipt of from .El5O, to .E2OO per year, and was entitled to one-twelfth of an estate valued at from £300,000 to .£400,000i a judgment summons was issued for the taxed costs, which, as plaintiff was already committed under another judgment, was dismissed. Mr. Davies stated that he had given notice to Messrs. Southern. and liar- wood, solicitors for the plaintiff (Edward Hart), of his intention to make the application, and they ' had replied that they should not attend the appli- cation.—His Honour said that he had no power under Order XVI., rule 22, to make an order for the payment out of court of the money, as that rule stated that the solicitor for the defendant would only have a lien for his costs in the action.---Mr. Davies submitted that by section IV., chap. 50, of the Act of Victoria, 3, his Honour ha el full power to make any order for the payment out of court of any money, as a judge in the high Court of Chambers would have.—His Honour thought that Mr. Davies was mistaken, as that section only gave him power to make an order at another court, such as he had power to make at his own court. if, however, the solicitors for the plaintiff would consent to the money being paid out, His Honour said he would make an order, although he did not think he had power to do so under the County Court rule of the Act cited.

At Montrose, on Wednesday, a lady got out of her depth while bathing. George Saxby, the keeper of the bathing place, went to her rescue on horseback; but the annnal lurched, and he was pitched into the water. Encumbered by his sea boots, the man sank and was drowned. It was with great difficulty that the lady was rescued. ARREST OF All M.P.—Mr. James ,O`Kelly, M.P., was arrested in London on Tuesday night on a warrant issued under the Crimes Act, and taken on Wednesday to Dublin. Before he was conveyed from town Mr. O'Kelly was visited by several members of the National- ist party. Mr. Jas. O'Kelly,.M P. was taken from Dublin to Boyle on Thursday, and brought before Mr. Turner, the resident magistrate, charged with takbag part in an un- lawful assembly, and also in a criminal conspiracy to in- duce certain persons not to give evidence at private in- quiries held by resident magistrates under the Crimes. Act. He was remanded until Wednesday, bail being al- lowed.

MR. BRADLAUGH AND HIS CONSTITTIENTS.—Mr. and- laugh, M.P., on Wednesday night addressed his con- stituents at Northampton in explanation of his action regarding the Oaths Bill. If the constituency condemned him, he said he would not continue to sit as their mem- ber. He justified his action in accepting the amend- ment to the bill on the ground that it would be impos- sible to pass it without the modifications proposed. lie would have preferred the bill as it was drafted, but he contended it accomplished more than anysiroilar measure yet submitted to Parliament.—A resolution was passed, with three dissentients, expressing confidence in Mr. Bradlaugh'a action,

div.head: SCARLET FEVER EPIDEMIC.
div.p: THE SCARLET FEVER EPIDEMIC.

Some fresh cases of scarlet fever have during the week been admitted to the Infectious Diseases Hospital at Warrington, and the total number of patients, most of whom are suffering from scarlet fever, in the hospital yesterday was 90. A portable wooden hospital tent, fitted up with beds and other conveniences, is expected to arrive at Warrington to-day (Saturday), to fill the need for further ac- commodation. The tent, which is supplied by a firm that supplied similar ones to the Preston Cor- poration recently, will accommodate 12 grown up people, or 20 children. There have, fortunately, been no more cases of smallpox, and one of the patients, the navvy who was first admitted, has been discharged cured. It is expected that another patient will be discharged to-day, in which case there will be only one smallpox patient under treatment. All the scarlet fever patients are doing well.
The mangers of the Ragged School have decided to close the school for four weeks in consequence of smallpox, and the epidemic of scarlet fever.

FRIENDLY SOClETlES.—Remarkable evidence was given before the Committee on the Friendly Societies Acts on Thursday as to the character and proceedings of some of the "collecting societies." It was stated that, althougla the official Registrar might be convinced of the unsound- ness of a society, ha had no power to prevent it from con- tinuing to receive money from the public. EXPLOSION ON BOARD a STEAM TRAWLER.—On Thurs- day morning four-of the crew of the steam trawler Pro- ceed, of Yarmouth, were brought into that port and conveyed to the hospital, suffering from severe scalds I about the face and body, the result of a boiler explosion. I The vessel was also damaged, but not so much as to pre. vent her being brought to port with the men on board. Mn. DILLON.—In the Irish EXcheguer Division, on 'Wednesday, before Chief Baron Niles, Mr. T. Healy, M.P., applied for a conditional order for habeas corpus to discharge Mr. John Dillon, M.P. from Dundalk gaoL The ground of application was that the County Court ludge had no jUrisdiction after the ease had been. deci- ded by the magistrates. A conditional order on this point was granted. THE ALLEGED ROBBERY OF £B,ooo.—At Bowkst , Lon- , don, on Thursday, Eddie Guerrin, alias George APCaull, alleged to be a notorious American burglar, was charged with stealing £B,OOO in notes from a bank at Lyons, by making off with a pocket-book while a clerk's back was turned. He was traced and captured in London. The magistrate remanded him. The men Bailey and Davies were again remanded at the same court charged with stealing £l,OOO at Munich. ' STOPPAGE OF THE RIBBLE DOCK WOW/S.—The Preston ' Town Council have decided to stop the Ribble dock works for twelve months, and to pay Mr. Walker, the contractor, £34,000 retention money, and £5,000 to keep the pump going, and see that the work done takes no harm. At the monthly mooting of the Preston Town Council, on /Thursday, there was much recrimination, and altogether a lively scene, about the Ribble scheme. The Corporation appears to have got into a deplorable position.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The inquest on Dr. Ridley stands adjourned until after the conclusion of the Mandeville inquest. Evictions were not resumed on the Vandeleur estate, on Friday, because of the inclement weather. CRICKBY. --- At Huddersfield, Yorkshire first innings closed for 107; Australians followed, and were all out for 48.

Justice Wills, referring to the Greenway case at the Warwick Assizes, on Friday, said there appeared to be a Serious charge aptinst George Greenway. Lord Knutsford yesterday afternoon unveiled a memo. rial tablet bearing a medallion portrait Of the late W. E. Forster which has been placed in Westminster Abbey: .
On-Friday morning his Royal Highness Prince Albert Victor, who is at present located in York with the 9th Hussars was presented with the freedom of the city by the Corporation.
Among the many marriages solemnised on Th-arsday wa.s that at the pro-Cathedral of Mr. C. Halle to Madame Norman Neruda. It was a quiet ceremony, and few people were aware.e.f it. _

deorge Timms, labourer, was indicted yesterday for murderinghis wife last January The jury found the prisoner guilty of murder whilst insane, and he was ordered to be detained during her Majesty's pleasure. THE Naval. MANamvßas.—The blockade of Admiral Fitzroy's Lough Switly squadron continues. A Lloyd's telegram on Friday reported that the attacking squadron is still outside the lough. Admiral Tryon's fleet in Ban- try Bay is also blockaded, and Admiral Baird's cruisers are still searching for the•cruiser Iris, which escaped. SCARLET FEVER Eprorunc.---Bolton has a scarlet fever epidemic, and the medical officer, in his report, issued on Friday, says that a house to house visitation revealed the fact that 22 families, obtaining milk from a certain farm, supplied 43 cases to the total. Some years ago Bolton was ravaged by disease arising fronacontaminated milk.

SUPPOSF.D DREADFUL TRAGEDY AT S&L—The Grimsby police have received particulars of a case which points to a brutal murder committed at sea, presumably on a fishing smack. The Grimsby smack Union, whilst fish-, ing with a Hull fleet, has brought up the body of a fish- ing youth, a mulatto, with, hands bound in irons, and skull frightfully battered in. _ .

DESPERATE POACHING APPAIR'IN CHESIIIRE.—EarIy on Friday morning, Inspector Johnson, of Northwich, and a posse of constables intercepted a numerous and well- armed gang of poachers who were returning to the town from Bostock Park. The poachers were most determined in their efforts to escape, and it was only after a terrible struggle that four of them were captured. 'FATAL FALL AT BURNLEY.-:-ShOTtly before ten o'clock on Friday morning, John Shaw, a middle-aged man, liv- ing at Augustus-st., Accrington, was killed at the Man- • chester-road station, Burnley. He went on, to the glass roof over the platform to take the measurement for a window, when one of the spars on which he knelt gave way and he fell upon his head on the platform 16 feet below. His skull was fractured, and he died in a few minutes.

div.head: ACCOUCHEMENT OF THE EMPRESS OF GERMANY. •
div.p: ACCOUCHEMENT OF THE EMPRESS OF GERMANY. •
_ The Empress was safely delivered of a son early on Friday morning. Her Majesty and the infant Prince are doing well. The Imperial couple have now five sons and no daughter. _
AFFAIRS IN ZULULAND.

DURBAN, FRIDAY.—The Transvaal Government, in formally notifying to Sir Arthur Havelock the union of the New Republic with the Transvaal, stated that meat-, sures would be taken to preserve strict neutrality as regards. Zululand. The total number of British troops in Zulidand is now 2,000. THE LO3S OF A FRENCH. SCHOONER AND

div.p: 20 LIVES.

The Germanic, whicii-reWched Queenstown yesterday, brings details of the sinking of a French schooner of Newfoundland with twenty hands by the steamer Fulda. The crew clung to the rigging, and one man attempted to climb on board the Fulda but fell back. The Fulda's boats cruised over the spot, but no trace of, the vessel or men could be discovered. '
YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT:. HOUSE OF LORDS.

Their Lordships met at four o'clock. • RIFLE SHOOTING, &C.—LOTCICADOGAN, replying to Lord Mount Temple, said the Government watched closely the sale of indecent publications.—Lerd Watoraoa-called attention to a petition presented to the First Commissioner of Works with 4,624 signatures in favour of National Rifle Association shooting in,Richmond Park. —The Duke of CAMBRIDGE said he objected in his capacity of Ranger. The time had come when such des- cription of shooting should take place away from resi- dences and gardens. The improved rifle made shooting more dangerous.—Lord SALISBURX said the matter was still under the consideration of the Government, with whom the responsibility of the decision. entinsly.rested. The House then adjourned: HOUSE OF COMMONS.. The Speaker took the chair at five. minutes past three o'clock. DR. BAR.R AND THE MANDEVILLE INQUEST.—MT. A. J. BALFOUR, in answer to Mr. Anderson, said unquestion- ably the Government would not suspend Dr. Barr.—Mr. HUNTER: Will the right. hon. gentleman give the house 'ah assurance that Dr. Barr shall not again visit Mr. John Dillon (loud Opposition cheers), having regard to the fatal consequences that followed his visits to Mr. Man- deville (Ministerial cries of "Oh,. ohs" and Opposition cheers.)—Mr. BALFOUR I can only say that Mr. John Dillon has the best medical advice. (Ironical Opposition cheers. . .

QUESTIONS.—Mr. E. STANHOPE, replying to, Mr. Roe, said it would be unwise to tie the War Office down to use any particular machine gun.—Mr. W. SMITH, reply- ing to sir W. Harcourt, said he hoped the consideration of the Local Government Bill would conclude that night, and the third reading be taken', if the House so agreed. LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL—The Expiring Laws Con- tinuance, Public Works Loans, and Metropolitan Board of Works Money Bills were read a first time. The Local Government Bill was further consklered as amended.— Mr. STANSFIELD moved an amendment to clause two to provide that the chairman of the Council should hold office for one, instead of three years, which was agreed to.—At the instance of Mr. SHAW LEFEVRE words were inserted in the twelfth clause giving County Councils the same powers as the Highway Boards for preventing and removing obstructions, andfor asserting the public rights for the use and enjoyment of roadside wastes.— Several proposed amendments were discussed and rejec- ted Guar moved an addition to clause 32 of the sub-section, enacting that it shoukl be lawful for the Queen, at any time on petition from, the Council of the borough, by .order in Council to declare such borough to be a county.—Mr. WATSON supported the amendment.—Mr. RITCHIE said the object of the amend- ment was to remove the 50,000ffimit of population for county boroughs. He would hold out no, hope of that figure being carried lower.—The amendment was nega- tived without a division. [LEFT SITTING.]

BRITISH WORKMAN'S ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED. Established 1866. Incorporated under the Companies Act, 1862, CRIF.F OFFICES : BROAD-ST. CORNER, BIRMINGHAM. EXTRACTS FROM THE DIRECTORS' REPORT for the year ending April 30th, 1888. Notwithstanding the liberal terms and conditions of the Company's Policies, and the heavy amount paid in claims,-and for extension expenses (resulting in the largest increase of new business the Company has ever made in any one year), the Directors are pleased to state that after meeting all pay- ments and expenses, they have been able to carry 'forward a balance exceeding £15,000. Mr. James Sketchley, one of your Directors, retired in De- cember last for the purpose of travelling, when Mr. J. C. Fowke, who for upwards of twenty years had been Solicitor to the Company, was requested by the Board to fill up the vacancy, which we are pleased to say he consented to do, and he has proved to be a very important addition to the director- ate. Mr. Fowke is not a shareholder, but holds a Policy in the Company upon his own life for £l,OOO, and therefore may be looked, upon as a more direct representative of the Policy holders. The total income of the Company for the year was £178,310 I.Bs Bd, being an increase of £21,928 its 9d. The total amount of payments was £163,018 148 id, leaving a balance upon the year's accounts of £15,292 4s 7d, making the total funds at the close of the year £96,302 19s Od. The amount paid in Claims during the year was £77,479, Including £4,411 6s Surrender Claims. The total sum paid up to the 30th April, 1888, was £469,261 le 10d. The number of Assurants upon the Company's books on the 30th April, 1888, was 374,098, and their annual premium would be £198,420 18s 10d, showing a net increase of 39,070 Assurants, and £27,820 us 9d in Premium Income. HENRY PORT, Managing Director. D. A. BECKETT, Secretary. DISTRICT OFFICE MARKET GATE CHAMBERS, WARRINGTON. S. GREEN, SUPERINTENDENT.
